subtopics.title: Arithmetic & Logical Operations
subtopics.subtitle: Signed integers, overflow, Booth multiplication, division, IEEE 754, shifts and BCD

concepts.text: Integer Representations

An n-bit register can hold an unsigned integer from 0 to 2^n − 1, or a signed integer if the most significant bit is used as a sign (0 = positive, 1 = negative). Three signed conventions exist. In sign-magnitude the remaining n − 1 bits hold the magnitude. In 1's complement a negative number is the bitwise inverse of the positive one. In 2's complement a negative number is the inverse plus 1, which is the same as 2^n − |x|. Practically every processor uses 2's complement because it has a single zero, subtraction is done with the same adder as addition, and the carry out of the sign position is simply discarded.
Addition, Subtraction and Overflow

A parallel (ripple-carry) adder is a chain of n full adders, the carry of each stage feeding the next; its delay grows with n, so wide ALUs use carry-lookahead logic that computes all carries from generate (G = AB) and propagate (P = A ⊕ B) signals in a fixed number of gate levels. An adder-subtractor adds one XOR gate per bit on the B input and a mode control M: with M = 0 the XORs pass B unchanged and the input carry is 0, so the circuit computes A + B; with M = 1 every B bit is complemented and the input carry is 1, so the circuit computes A + B' + 1 = A − B in 2's complement. Comparison (A − B) uses the same hardware and only the flags are kept.
Overflow in signed (2's complement) arithmetic:
items: Overflow can occur only when two numbers of the same sign are added (or numbers of opposite sign are subtracted); the result then shows the wrong sign. Adding numbers of opposite sign can never overflow.
Hardware test: V = C_n ⊕ C_(n−1), the XOR of the carry out of the sign bit and the carry into the sign bit. V = 1 means the result is invalid.
Worked example, 4 bits: 0111 (+7) + 0001 (+1) = 1000 (−8). C4 = 0 and C3 = 1, so V = 1: overflow. Also 1000 (−8) + 1111 (−1) = 0111 (+7) with C4 = 1, C3 = 0: overflow.

Unsigned overflow is different: it is signalled by the carry out C_n alone. The ALU sets both the carry flag and the overflow flag; the program picks the one that matches how it interprets the operands.
In 1's complement arithmetic the carry out is not discarded but added back into the LSB (end-around carry), one reason 1's complement lost out to 2's complement.

concepts.plainText: V = C_n XOR C_(n−1) (carry out of sign bit XOR carry into sign bit)

concepts.text: Multiplication and Division

Unsigned multiplication is done by shift-and-add. The multiplicand is in register B, the multiplier in Q, an accumulator A is cleared and a counter is set to n. Each step examines the least significant bit of Q: if it is 1, B is added to A; then the pair (A, Q) is shifted right one place and the counter is decremented. After n steps the 2n-bit product sits in A:Q. Sign-magnitude numbers are multiplied by multiplying magnitudes and XOR-ing the sign bits. Booth's algorithm multiplies 2's complement numbers directly, without sign correction, by treating a run of 1s in the multiplier from bit j to bit k as 2^(k+1) − 2^j, so it only adds or subtracts at the ends of runs and can be faster when the multiplier has long runs of identical bits.
Booth's algorithm (multiplicand M, multiplier in Q, accumulator A = 0, an extra bit Q−1 = 0, counter = n):
items: Look at the pair Q0 Q−1. If it is 1 0, do A ← A − M. If it is 0 1, do A ← A + M. If it is 0 0 or 1 1, do nothing.
Arithmetic-shift right the triple (A, Q, Q−1) one place: the sign bit of A is copied, the old Q0 moves into Q−1.
Decrement the counter; repeat until it reaches 0. The signed 2n-bit product is in A:Q; Q−1 is discarded.
Number of add/subtract operations equals the number of 0→1 and 1→0 transitions in the multiplier, not the number of 1s.

concepts.text: Division of unsigned or magnitude numbers uses shift-and-subtract. In restoring division the dividend pair (A, Q) is shifted left, the divisor M is subtracted from A, and the new quotient bit Q0 is set to 1 if the result is non-negative; if it is negative Q0 is set to 0 and M is added back (restored). After n steps Q holds the quotient and A the remainder. Non-restoring division avoids the restore: if A is negative, the next step shifts and adds M instead of subtracting, and a single correction (add M if A is still negative) is made at the end, so it needs one add or subtract per bit instead of up to two. Before starting, the hardware checks for divide-by-zero and for divide overflow, which occurs when the high half of the dividend is greater than or equal to the divisor, so the quotient would not fit in n bits.
Floating-Point Representation (IEEE 754)
IEEE 754 single precision packs a real number into 32 bits as sign, biased exponent and fraction:
items: Fields: 1 sign bit S, 8 exponent bits E with bias 127 (stored E = true exponent + 127), 23 fraction bits F. A normalised number has an implied leading 1, so the significand is 1.F and the effective precision is 24 bits. Double precision uses 1/11/52 with bias 1023.

Special encodings: E = 0 and F = 0 is ±0; E = 0 and F ≠ 0 is a denormalised (subnormal) number with no hidden 1; E = 255 and F = 0 is ±infinity; E = 255 and F ≠ 0 is NaN. Normalised exponents therefore run from 1 to 254, true exponents −126 to +127.
Range: roughly ±1.18 × 10^−38 to ±3.4 × 10^38 for single precision; about 7 significant decimal digits (15–16 for double).

Worked encoding of −6.5: 6.5 = 110.1 in binary = 1.101 × 2^2. S = 1; E = 2 + 127 = 129 = 1000 0001; F = 101 followed by twenty 0s. The word is 1 10000001 10100000000000000000000 = C0D0 0000 in hexadecimal.
Decoding: value = (−1)^S × 1.F × 2^(E − 127). A bigger bias-coded exponent field means a bigger number, so floating-point values of the same sign can be compared like sign-magnitude integers.

concepts.plainText: x = (−1)^S × 1.F × 2^(E − 127) for a normalised IEEE 754 single-precision number

concepts.text: Floating-point arithmetic is done on the sign, exponent and mantissa parts separately:
items: Addition/subtraction: check for zero operands; align the exponents by shifting the mantissa of the smaller number right by the exponent difference; add or subtract the mantissas; normalise the result (shift and adjust the exponent); round to the available bits; check exponent overflow or underflow.

Multiplication: add the exponents and subtract one bias; multiply the mantissas; sign = S1 ⊕ S2; normalise and round. Division: subtract the exponents and add the bias; divide the mantissas; sign = S1 ⊕ S2; normalise and round.
Guard, round and sticky bits are kept beyond the mantissa during the operation so that rounding (default: round to nearest, ties to even) is accurate.
Alignment can lose all the bits of a much smaller operand, so floating-point addition is not associative: (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c).

concepts.text: BCD (binary-coded decimal) arithmetic stores each decimal digit in 4 bits (0000 to 1001), so the codes 1010 to 1111 are invalid. Two BCD digits are added with an ordinary 4-bit binary adder; if the binary sum is greater than 9 or the adder produces a carry, 0110 (6) is added to skip the six unused codes and generate the decimal carry. For example 8 + 5: 1000 + 0101 = 1101 (13, invalid), add 0110 → 1 0011, which reads as carry 1 and digit 3. A decimal adder is therefore a binary adder plus this correction logic, and a k-digit BCD adder cascades k of them. BCD subtraction is done by adding the 9's or 10's complement of the subtrahend. BCD is used where exact decimal results matter (calculators, financial software, display drivers) at the cost of speed and storage.
Going Deeper: Arithmetic Algorithms Step by Step

Mano's sign-magnitude adder-subtractor keeps the magnitudes in registers A and B, their signs in As and Bs, the end carry in flip-flop E and an overflow flag AVF. Subtraction is first turned into addition by complementing Bs, after which only two cases remain. If the signs are equal, the magnitudes are added and the end carry is copied into AVF as the overflow indication. If the signs differ, A + B' + 1 is formed: E = 1 means A ≥ B and the result is already correct, while E = 0 means A < B, so A is replaced by its 2's complement and As is complemented. When the magnitudes cancel (A = B), As is cleared so that the result is +0, never −0.

rows: A ← A + B' + 1, then A ← A' + 1

concepts.plainText: Q·M = Σ (q_(i−1) − q_i)·2^i·M over i = 0 … n−1, with q_(−1) = 0: pair Q0 Q−1 = 10 gives −M, 01 gives +M, 00 and 11 give nothing

concepts.text: The recoded digit q_(i−1) − q_i is −1 at the right-hand end of a run of 1s, +1 just past its left-hand end and 0 inside a run of 1s or of 0s. Summed over all positions, these digits reproduce the 2's complement weight −2^(n−1) of the sign bit automatically, so Booth's algorithm needs no sign correction, provided the partial product is kept signed by an arithmetic right shift. The worst case is an alternating multiplier such as 0101 0101, which needs an operation in every cycle; bit-pair (radix-4) recoding looks at two bits at a time, uses the digits −2 to +2 and halves the number of partial products. The table multiplies M = 0111 (+7) by Q = 1101 (−3).

Restoring division of 1011 (11) by 0011 (3), tabulated below, keeps the dividend in Q, the divisor in M = 00011 and a 5-bit partial remainder A that starts at 00000, the extra bit showing the sign of A − M. Each cycle shifts A and Q left as one register, subtracts M, and keeps the difference only if it is not negative (q0 = 1); otherwise q0 = 0 and M is added back. Non-restoring division skips the add-back: when A is negative, the next cycle shifts and adds M, because 2(A + M) − M = 2A + M, and after n cycles one correction A ← A + M is made if A is still negative. Both methods leave the quotient in Q and the remainder in A.

concepts.text: Common slips: using a logical instead of an arithmetic right shift in Booth's algorithm; forgetting that the restoring divider's A register needs an extra bit for the sign; reading the carry flag as signed overflow; forgetting the hidden 1 when decoding IEEE 754, or storing it in F when encoding; adding both biases, or neither, when multiplying floating-point numbers; and applying the BCD +6 correction only when the 4-bit sum exceeds 9 while ignoring the case where the adder itself produced a carry (8 + 9 = 1 0001). One special case: with an n-bit A register, Booth's algorithm gives wrong products when the multiplicand is −2^(n−1) (1000 in 4 bits), because −M does not fit in n bits; one extra bit in A and M removes the problem.

formulas.plainText: Range of an n-bit 2's complement integer: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1
Signed overflow flag: V = C_n XOR C_(n−1)
2's complement of x: invert all bits and add 1, equal to 2^n − x
IEEE 754 single precision: x = (−1)^S × 1.F × 2^(E − 127)

notes.text: For the 2's complement of a number: copy the bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest. 0101 1000 → 1010 1000. This is faster and less error-prone than invert-and-add-1 in the exam.

Carry and overflow are different flags. In 2's complement addition ignore the carry out and check V = C_n ⊕ C_(n−1); a carry out of 1 does not by itself mean the signed result is wrong, and a carry out of 0 does not mean it is right.
Booth's algorithm needs the extra Q−1 bit and an arithmetic (sign-preserving) right shift; the plain shift-and-add multiplier uses a logical shift and works only for unsigned or magnitude values.
IEEE 754 numbers to remember: single 1/8/23 with bias 127, double 1/11/52 with bias 1023, hidden leading 1 in normalised numbers, all-1s exponent means infinity or NaN.

flashcards.front: Why do processors use 2's complement rather than sign-magnitude or 1's complement?
flashcards.back: It has a single representation of zero, subtraction is performed by the same adder (A + B' + 1), and the carry out of the sign bit is simply discarded with no end-around correction.

flashcards.front: What does Booth's algorithm do on each of the Q0 Q−1 bit pairs 10, 01, 00 and 11?
flashcards.back: 10: A ← A − M; 01: A ← A + M; 00 or 11: no arithmetic. In every case the triple (A, Q, Q−1) is then arithmetic-shifted right one place.

flashcards.front: Difference between a logical, an arithmetic and a circular right shift?
flashcards.back: Logical fills the vacated MSB with 0; arithmetic copies the sign bit into it (divide by 2 for signed numbers); circular (rotate) moves the bit shifted out of the LSB back into the MSB.

questions.questionText: Using Booth's algorithm to multiply the 4-bit 2's complement numbers +3 (0011) and −4 (1100) with −4 as the multiplier, how many add/subtract operations are performed and what is the 8-bit product?
questions.explanation: The multiplier 1100 with Q−1 = 0 gives pairs 00, 00, 10, 11 over the four cycles, so only one subtraction (A ← A − M) occurs. The final A:Q is 1111 0100 = −12.

questions.questionText: In IEEE 754 single-precision format, what is the stored exponent field for the number 6.5?
questions.explanation: 6.5 = 110.1 in binary = 1.101 × 2^2, so the true exponent is 2 and the stored value is 2 + 127 = 129 = 1000 0001.

questions.questionText: In a 4-bit adder-subtractor built from full adders with an XOR gate on each B input and a mode control M, subtraction A − B is obtained by:
options: M = 1, so B is complemented and the input carry is 1, giving A + B' + 1
M = 1, so B is complemented and the input carry is 0, giving A + B'
M = 0, so B is complemented by the full adders internally
M = 1, so A is complemented and the result is then negated
questions.explanation: With M = 1 each XOR outputs B', and M is also fed as the input carry C0 = 1, so the sum is A + B' + 1, which is A plus the 2's complement of B, i.e. A − B.

questions.questionText: What is the 8-bit 2's complement representation of −44?
questions.explanation: +44 = 0010 1100; inverting gives 1101 0011 (the 1's complement) and adding 1 gives 1101 0100. 1010 1100 is the sign-magnitude form.

questions.questionText: What is the range of a 12-bit 2's complement integer?
questions.explanation: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1 with n = 12 gives −2048 to +2047. −2047 to +2047 is the sign-magnitude or 1's complement range, and 0 to 4095 is the unsigned range.

questions.questionText: The 8-bit 2's complement numbers 0100 1011 (+75) and 0101 1010 (+90) are added. What are the 8-bit result, the carry out C and the overflow flag V?
questions.explanation: The true sum 165 exceeds +127, and the 8 bits read 1010 0101 (−91). The carry into the sign bit is 1 and the carry out of it is 0, so V = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1 while C = 0.

questions.questionText: The 8-bit 2's complement subtraction A − B, with A = 1010 0000 (−96) and B = 0100 0000 (+64), is performed as A + B' + 1. What are the result, the carry out C and the overflow flag V?
questions.explanation: B' + 1 = 1100 0000, and 1010 0000 + 1100 0000 = 1 0110 0000, so C = 1 and the 8 bits read +96. The true answer −160 is below −128: the carry into the sign bit (0) differs from the carry out (1), so V = 1. 1110 0000 is A + B, and 0101 1111 forgets the +1.

questions.questionText: In 2's complement addition, overflow can never occur when:
options: The two operands have opposite signs
The carry out of the sign bit is 1
questions.explanation: A sum of numbers with opposite signs lies between the two operands, so it always fits. Two positives or two negatives can overflow, and a carry out of 1 on its own says nothing about signed overflow.

questions.questionText: In 8-bit 1's complement arithmetic, what is the result of adding 0000 1001 (+9) and 1111 1010 (−5)?
questions.explanation: 0000 1001 + 1111 1010 = 1 0000 0011. In 1's complement the end carry is added back into the LSB (end-around carry): 0000 0011 + 1 = 0000 0100 = +4. Discarding the carry as in 2's complement would give 0000 0011 (+3).

questions.questionText: Mano's sign-magnitude adder-subtractor computes (+5) − (+9) with 4-bit magnitudes A = 0101 and B = 1001. The magnitudes are subtracted as A + B' + 1 into E and A. What are the end carry E and the final result?
options: E = 0; A = 1100 is replaced by its 2's complement 0100 and the sign is changed, giving −4
E = 0; the result is −1100 (−12), taken directly from A
questions.explanation: Like signs in a subtraction mean the magnitudes are subtracted: 0101 + 0110 + 1 = 0 1100, so E = 0, which shows A < B. Mano's algorithm then forms A' + 1 (1100 → 0100) and complements As, giving −0100 = −4.

questions.questionText: In Mano's sign-magnitude addition and subtraction hardware, when is the overflow flip-flop AVF set to 1?
options: Whenever the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of it
Whenever the magnitudes are subtracted and E = 0
When the magnitudes are added and the end carry E is 1
Whenever the sign of the result differs from the sign of B
questions.explanation: The sign bits do not pass through the adder in sign-magnitude hardware; overflow is possible only when magnitudes are added, and the end carry, copied into AVF, shows it. When magnitudes are subtracted, E only tells whether A ≥ B and AVF is cleared.

questions.questionText: In a carry-lookahead adder with generate G_i = A_i B_i and propagate P_i = A_i ⊕ B_i, the carry into stage i + 1 is:
questions.explanation: A stage produces a carry if it generates one (both inputs 1) or if it propagates an incoming carry (exactly one input 1 and C_i = 1). Expanding recursively, e.g. C2 = G1 + P1G0 + P1P0C0, gives every carry in two gate levels after G and P.

questions.questionText: Which statement about 2's complement arithmetic is NOT correct?
options: There is only one representation of zero
A carry out of the sign bit always means that the signed result has overflowed
A − B can be computed as A + B' + 1 with the same adder
The range contains one more negative value than positive values
questions.explanation: In 2's complement the carry out is discarded and overflow is V = C_n ⊕ C_(n−1). For example (−1) + (−1) = 1111 + 1111 = 1 1110 has a carry out, yet the 4-bit result −2 is correct.

questions.questionText: An unsigned shift-and-add multiplier (Mano) multiplies B = 1101 (13) by Q = 1011 (11). A = 0000 and E = 0 at the start; in each cycle B is added to A (carry into E) if Q0 = 1, then E, A and Q are shifted right one place together. What are A and Q after the second cycle?
questions.explanation: Cycle 1: Q0 = 1, A = 1101; shift → A = 0110, Q = 1101. Cycle 2: Q0 = 1, EA = 0110 + 1101 = 1 0011; shifting E, A and Q right gives A = 1001, Q = 1110. After four cycles A:Q = 1000 1111 = 143.

questions.questionText: An unsigned shift-and-add multiplier multiplies two 8-bit numbers. How many add-and-shift cycles are needed, and how wide must the product register be?
questions.explanation: One cycle handles each multiplier bit, so n = 8 cycles, and the product of two n-bit numbers needs up to 2n = 16 bits (255 × 255 = 65 025 < 2^16).

questions.questionText: In Booth's algorithm with the 4-bit multiplier Q = 0111 (+7) and Q−1 = 0 at the start, which arithmetic operations are performed in the four cycles?
options: Subtract M in cycle 1 and add M in cycle 4
Add M in cycle 1 and subtract M in cycle 4
questions.explanation: The pairs Q0 Q−1 seen in the four cycles are 10, 11, 11 and 01: subtract M in cycle 1, nothing in cycles 2 and 3, and add M in cycle 4. This computes 8M − M = 7M.

questions.questionText: Booth's algorithm multiplies M = 0101 (+5) by Q = 1010 (−6) in 4 bits, starting with A = 0000 and Q−1 = 0. What are A, Q and Q−1 after the second cycle, including its shift?
questions.explanation: Cycle 1: Q0 Q−1 = 00, shift only → A = 0000, Q = 0101, Q−1 = 0. Cycle 2: Q0 Q−1 = 10, A ← A − M = 1011, then an arithmetic shift right gives A = 1101, Q = 1010, Q−1 = 1 (a logical shift would wrongly give A = 0101). The final A:Q is 1110 0010 = −30.

questions.questionText: Booth's algorithm multiplies the 4-bit 2's complement numbers M = 1010 (−6) and Q = 1011 (−5). What is the final 8-bit product in A:Q?
questions.explanation: The pairs Q0 Q−1 over the four cycles are 10, 11, 01 and 10 (subtract, none, add, subtract), ending with A:Q = 0001 1110 = +30 = (−6) × (−5). 1110 0010 is −30, and 0110 1110 (110) is what an unsigned multiplier gives for 1010 × 1011.

questions.questionText: For which 8-bit multiplier does Booth's algorithm perform the largest number of add/subtract operations?
questions.explanation: Booth adds or subtracts once for each 0→1 or 1→0 transition in the multiplier with Q−1 = 0 appended. 0101 0101 needs 8 operations, 1111 1111 needs 1, and 0000 1111 and 0111 1110 need 2 each.

questions.questionText: Bit-pair recoding (radix-4 modified Booth) of the multiplier is used in a 16 × 16-bit signed multiplier. At most how many partial products (summands) must be added?
questions.explanation: Each pair of multiplier bits is recoded into one digit from {−2, −1, 0, +1, +2}, so a 16-bit multiplier gives 16/2 = 8 summands instead of 16, each a shifted and/or negated copy of the multiplicand.

questions.questionText: Restoring division of the 4-bit dividend 1101 (13) by the divisor 0100 (4) uses a 5-bit register A (initially 00000), Q = 1101 and M = 00100. Each cycle shifts A and Q left, subtracts M from A and then either sets Q0 = 1 or sets Q0 = 0 and restores A. What are A and Q after the third cycle?
questions.explanation: Cycles 1 and 2 give a negative A − M, so q0 = 0 and A is restored (A = 00001 then 00011; Q = 1010 then 0100). Cycle 3: after the shift A = 00110, A − M = 00010 is not negative, so q0 = 1 and Q = 1001. After cycle 4 the quotient is 0011 (3) and the remainder 00001 (1).

questions.questionText: Non-restoring division of 1110 (14) by 0101 (5) uses a 5-bit A (initially 00000), Q = 1110 and M = 00101. After the four cycles, what are Q and A, and what happens next?
options: Q = 0010 and A = 11111 is negative, so M is added once more, giving the remainder 00100
Q = 0010 and A = 00100, so no correction is needed
Q = 0011 and A = 11111, so the quotient is incremented to 0100
Q = 0010 and A = 11111, which is kept as the remainder −1
questions.explanation: The four cycles do A − M = 11100 (q0 = 0), A + M = 11110 (q0 = 0), A + M = 00010 (q0 = 1) and A − M = 11111 (q0 = 0). Q = 0010 = 2, and because A is negative the remainder is corrected: 11111 + 00101 = 00100 = 4, since 14 = 2 × 5 + 4.

questions.questionText: Which statement about non-restoring division is correct?
options: It never needs a correction step at the end
When A becomes negative, the next cycle shifts and adds M instead of restoring and then subtracting, so each cycle needs only one addition or subtraction
It produces two quotient bits in every cycle
It can be used only when the dividend is smaller than the divisor
questions.explanation: Restoring and then shifting and subtracting, 2(A + M) − M, equals shifting and adding, 2A + M, so the restore can be skipped. A final correction A ← A + M is still needed when the last remainder is negative.

questions.questionText: A divider for 4-bit divisors takes an 8-bit dividend in A:Q. The dividend 0111 0000 (112) is to be divided by 0110 (6). What does Mano's divide-overflow check conclude?
options: No overflow: the quotient 18 and remainder 4 are produced normally
Divide overflow: the high half 0111 is not less than the divisor 0110, so the quotient will not fit in 4 bits
No overflow, because the divisor is not zero
No overflow, because A and Q together hold 8 bits, enough for the quotient 1 0010
questions.explanation: If A ≥ B before division starts, the quotient would be at least 2^n. Here 112/6 = 18 > 15, so the divide-overflow flag DVF is set and the division is not carried out.

questions.questionText: For 16-bit operands, what is the largest number of add/subtract operations in the main loop of restoring division that restores a negative A by adding M back (as in the Stallings and Hamacher flowcharts), and of non-restoring division (not counting its final correction)?
questions.explanation: Restoring division subtracts in each of the 16 cycles and may have to restore with an addition in each, up to 2 × 16 = 32 operations; non-restoring division performs exactly one addition or subtraction per cycle, 16 in all, plus at most one correction. A non-performing restoring divider, which simply keeps the old A instead of adding M back, would need at most 16.

questions.questionText: What is the IEEE 754 single-precision encoding of −0.3125, in hexadecimal?
questions.explanation: 0.3125 = 0.0101 (binary) = 1.01 × 2^−2, so S = 1, E = −2 + 127 = 125 = 0111 1101 and F = 0100…0, giving 1 01111101 0100…0 = BEA0 0000. 3EA0 0000 is +0.3125, BF20 0000 has the exponent one too large (−0.625) and BED0 0000 stores the hidden 1 in F.

questions.questionText: What decimal value does the IEEE 754 single-precision word 4148 0000 (hex) represent?
What is the IEEE 754 double-precision encoding of 1.0, in hexadecimal?
In IEEE 754 single precision, what does the bit pattern 7F80 0000 (hex) represent?
questions.explanation: 7F80 0000 = 0 11111111 000…0: an all-1s exponent with a zero fraction is infinity, and S = 0 makes it +∞. A non-zero fraction would be NaN, and the largest finite number is 7F7F FFFF.

questions.questionText: What is the smallest positive number representable in IEEE 754 single precision, including denormalised numbers?
questions.explanation: A denormal has E = 0, no hidden 1 and scale 2^−126, so the smallest one is 0.00…01 (23 fraction bits) × 2^−126 = 2^−23 × 2^−126 = 2^−149 ≈ 1.4 × 10^−45. 2^−126 is the smallest normalised number.

questions.questionText: How many bits of significand precision, including the hidden bit, does an IEEE 754 double-precision number have?
questions.explanation: Double precision stores 52 fraction bits and the normalised form adds an implied leading 1, giving 53 bits of precision, about 15–16 decimal digits. 11 is the exponent width and 64 the total word length.

questions.questionText: Using the default round-to-nearest-even mode, what is the IEEE 754 single-precision encoding of 0.1, in hexadecimal?
questions.explanation: 0.1 = 1.1001 1001 1001… × 2^−4, so E = 123 = 0111 1011. The first 23 fraction bits are 1001 1001 1001 1001 1001 100 and the bits after them (1100…) are more than half a unit in the last place, so the fraction is rounded up to …101, giving 3DCC CCCD. Truncation gives 3DCC CCCC, while 3E4C CCCD is 0.2 and 3D4C CCCD is 0.05.

questions.questionText: A floating-point addition produces the unnormalised result 0.0011 × 2^6 (binary significand). To normalise it to the 1.F form, the significand is:
options: Shifted right 3 places and the exponent becomes 9
Shifted left 3 places and the exponent becomes 3
Shifted left 2 places and the exponent becomes 4
Shifted left 3 places and the exponent becomes 9
questions.explanation: 0.0011 × 2^6 = 1.1 × 2^3: moving the leading 1 to the left of the binary point is a left shift of the significand by 3, so the exponent must decrease by 3, from 6 to 3 (both equal 12).

questions.questionText: In IEEE 754 double precision, what is the stored 11-bit exponent field of a number whose true exponent is −10?
questions.explanation: Stored exponent = true exponent + 1023 = −10 + 1023 = 1013 = 011 1111 0101. 100 0000 1001 (1033) is for +10, 000 0111 0101 is the single-precision value 117, and 111 1111 0110 is the 11-bit 2's complement of −10, which IEEE 754 does not use.

questions.questionText: Two floating-point numbers with binary significands, X = 1.100 × 2^3 and Y = 1.010 × 2^1, are added. After alignment, addition and normalisation, the result is:
questions.explanation: Align Y to the larger exponent by shifting its significand right 3 − 1 = 2 places: 1.010 × 2^1 = 0.0101 × 2^3. Then 1.1000 + 0.0101 = 1.1101, already normalised, so the sum is 1.1101 × 2^3 = 14.5 (12 + 2.5). Adding without alignment gives 1.0110 × 2^4, and shifting by only 1 place gives 1.0001 × 2^4.

questions.questionText: Two IEEE 754 single-precision numbers with stored (biased) exponents 130 and 125 are multiplied. Before any normalisation, what is the stored exponent of the product?
questions.explanation: Each stored exponent contains the bias 127, so one bias must be removed from the sum: 130 + 125 − 127 = 128 (true exponents 3 + (−2) = 1). 255 forgets to subtract the bias, 1 subtracts it twice and 5 subtracts the exponents as in division.

questions.questionText: What is the product of the IEEE 754 single-precision numbers 4040 0000 (hex) and BF00 0000 (hex), as a single-precision hex word?
Which step is NOT part of floating-point multiplication?
options: Adding the exponents and subtracting the bias
Aligning the significands by shifting the one with the smaller exponent
Setting the result sign to the XOR of the operand signs
questions.explanation: Alignment is needed only for addition and subtraction, where the exponents must be made equal. Multiplication adds the exponents, multiplies the significands, XORs the signs and then normalises and rounds.

questions.questionText: Why does IEEE 754 store the exponent in biased (excess) form rather than in 2's complement?
options: Because a biased exponent has a larger range than a 2's complement exponent of the same width
Because the hardware cannot add 2's complement exponents
So that the hidden bit can be stored in the exponent field
So that floating-point numbers of the same sign can be compared like unsigned integers, with the all-zero word representing zero
questions.explanation: With a bias the smallest exponent is all 0s and the largest all 1s, so larger magnitudes have larger bit patterns and integer comparison hardware can be used; 0.0 is the all-zero word. Both codings give 2^k exponent patterns, so the range is not the reason.

questions.questionText: What is the BCD (8421) representation of the decimal number 739?
questions.explanation: Each decimal digit is coded separately in 4 bits: 7 = 0111, 3 = 0011, 9 = 1001. 0010 1110 0011 is the pure binary value of 739, 1010 0110 1100 is excess-3 and 1001 0011 0111 reverses the digits.

questions.questionText: The BCD numbers 0100 0111 (47) and 0011 1000 (38) are added with 4-bit binary adders and the standard BCD correction. What is the corrected result?
questions.explanation: Units: 0111 + 1000 = 1111 (15 > 9), so add 0110 → 1 0101, giving digit 5 and a carry of 1. Tens: 0100 + 0011 + 1 = 1000 (8) needs no correction, so the result is 1000 0101 = 85. 0111 1111 is the uncorrected binary sum and 1110 0101 corrects both digits.

questions.questionText: Two BCD digits 1001 (9) and 1001 (9) are added in a 4-bit binary adder, which gives a carry of 1 and sum bits 0010. What correction is required, and what is the BCD result?
options: No correction, because 0010 is a valid BCD digit; the result is 0001 0010 (12)
Add 0110 to the tens digit only; the result is 0111 0010
Add 0110, because the adder produced a carry; the result is 0001 1000 (18)
Add 0011 (the excess-3 correction); the result is 0001 0101 (15)
questions.explanation: The correction is needed when the 4-bit sum exceeds 9 or when the adder itself produces a carry. 9 + 9 = 1 0010 in binary; adding 0110 to 0010 gives 1000, so the result is tens digit 1 and units digit 8, 0001 1000.

questions.questionText: The BCD subtraction 72 − 35 is carried out by adding the 10's complement of the subtrahend. What is that 10's complement, and what is the result after the end carry is discarded?
questions.explanation: The 10's complement of 35 is 99 − 35 + 1 = 65. 72 + 65 = 137, and discarding the end carry leaves 37, a positive result because a carry appeared. 64 is the 9's complement, which needs the end-around carry to reach 37.

questions.questionText: Why is 0110 added when a 4-bit BCD sum exceeds 9?
options: To convert the sum to excess-3 code
To form the 9's complement of the sum
To clear the carry flag before the next digit is added
To skip the six unused codes 1010 to 1111 so that the correct decimal digit and decimal carry are produced
questions.explanation: A 4-bit adder counts in base 16 while BCD counts in base 10; adding 6 jumps over the six invalid codes, which wraps the digit back into 0 to 9 and generates the decimal carry.

questions.questionText: Registers hold A = 1101 1010 and B = 1111 0000. What is the result of the selective-clear micro-operation A ← A ∧ B'?
questions.explanation: B' = 0000 1111, so A ∧ B' keeps A's low four bits and clears the bits where B has 1s: 0000 1010. 1101 0000 is the mask A ∧ B, 1111 1010 is A ∨ B and 0010 1010 is A ⊕ B.

questions.questionText: Using Mano's insert operation, the upper four bits of A = 0110 1010 are to be replaced by 1001 while the lower four bits are kept. Which sequence of micro-operations does this, and what is the result?
options: AND A with 0000 1111, then OR with 1001 0000; A = 1001 1010
AND A with 1111 0000, then OR with 0000 1001; A = 0110 1001
questions.explanation: Insert is a mask followed by an OR: A ∧ 0000 1111 = 0000 1010 clears the field and OR with 1001 0000 sets the new bits, giving 1001 1010. An OR or XOR alone cannot clear the 1s already in the field, and the last choice replaces the lower four bits instead.

questions.questionText: What is the result of an arithmetic shift right (ashr) of the 8-bit 2's complement number 1011 0110 (−74)?
questions.explanation: ashr copies the sign bit into the vacated MSB and drops the LSB: 1011 0110 → 1101 1011 = −37, a division by 2. A logical shift right inserts 0 (0101 1011), 0110 1100 is a left shift and 1110 1101 is a two-place shift.

questions.questionText: An arithmetic shift left (ashl) is applied to the 8-bit 2's complement number 1110 0110 (−26). What are the result and the overflow flag V?
questions.explanation: ashl shifts every bit left and inserts 0: 1110 0110 → 1100 1100 = −52 = 2 × (−26). Mano's overflow test is V = A7 ⊕ A6 before the shift = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: a 1 is shifted out but the sign does not change, so there is no overflow. 1100 1101 is a circular shift (cil) and 1111 0011 an arithmetic shift right.

questions.questionText: A = 1001 0011 and the carry flag C = 0. After one rotate left through carry, what are A and C?
questions.explanation: In a rotate through carry the MSB (1) moves into C and the old C (0) enters the LSB, so A = 0010 0110 and C = 1. 0010 0111 is a plain circular shift left (cil), where the MSB goes straight to the LSB, and 1100 1001 is a circular shift right.

subtopics.title: Memory Hierarchy, Internal & External Memory
subtopics.subtitle: Hierarchy and locality, SRAM/DRAM/ROM, error correction, disks, RAID, SSD and tape

concepts.text: The Memory Hierarchy

No single memory technology is at the same time fast, large and cheap: faster memory costs more per bit and therefore comes in smaller sizes. A computer therefore uses a hierarchy of levels. Moving down the pyramid from registers to tape, the access time increases, the cost per bit decreases, the capacity increases and the frequency with which the processor accesses that level decreases. The design goal is to give the processor the average speed of the top levels at close to the cost per bit of the bottom levels, which works because programs obey the principle of locality of reference.
Locality of reference, the property that makes the hierarchy work:
items: Temporal locality: a location referenced now is likely to be referenced again soon (loop bodies, counters, stack variables). Keeping the item in a faster level after first use pays off.
Spatial locality: locations near a referenced address are likely to be referenced soon (sequential instructions, array elements). Fetching a whole block or line at once exploits this.
Sequential locality is the special case of spatial locality where the next reference is the next address, typical of instruction fetch.
Because of locality the hit ratio h of an upper level is high (often above 0.9), so the average access time is close to that of the fast level even though most data live in the slow one.

concepts.text: Internal Memory: RAM

rows: Required periodically (about every 64 ms) as the charge leaks
Cache memory, register files, small embedded RAM

concepts.text: A DRAM chip arranges its cells in a square array of rows and columns. To halve the number of address pins the address is multiplexed: the row half is latched by the RAS (row address strobe) signal and the column half by CAS (column address strobe), so a 16M × 1 chip needs only 12 address pins for its 24-bit address. Reading a cell discharges its capacitor, so the sense amplifiers immediately rewrite the whole row; refresh is done by reading every row in turn within the retention period (for example 4096 rows in 64 ms), during which the chip is unavailable. A DRAM is therefore slower in cycle time than in access time, and needs a memory controller to generate RAS, CAS and refresh cycles.

Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) ties the memory to the system clock: the processor issues the address and control signals, and after a known number of clock cycles (the CAS latency) the data appear, so the processor can do other work instead of waiting; burst mode then streams successive words one per clock without further addresses. Double data rate (DDR) SDRAM transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges, doubling the bandwidth at the same clock; DDR2, DDR3, DDR4 and DDR5 raise the prefetch width and transfer rate while lowering the supply voltage. Memory modules (DIMMs) place several chips side by side to provide a 64-bit wide data path.

rows: User once, with a programmer that blows fuses
Ultraviolet light through a quartz window, whole chip, minutes
Electrically, one block (sector) at a time
SSDs, USB drives, BIOS/UEFI, microcontroller program memory

concepts.text: Error detection and correction in memory:
items: Parity: one extra bit per word makes the number of 1s even (even parity) or odd (odd parity). It detects any single-bit error but cannot locate it and misses double-bit errors.

Hamming single-error-correcting (SEC) code: k check bits are added to m data bits such that 2^k ≥ m + k + 1. Each check bit is the parity of a chosen subset of positions; the check bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, … of the code word.

On a read the check bits are recomputed and XOR-ed with the stored ones. The result, the syndrome, is 0 if there is no error, otherwise it equals the position of the flipped bit, which is then inverted.
Check bits needed: 8 data bits → 4, 16 → 5, 32 → 6, 64 → 7. Adding one more overall parity bit gives SEC-DED (single error correcting, double error detecting), the scheme used in ECC memory modules.

concepts.plainText: Hamming SEC: k check bits for m data bits need 2^k ≥ m + k + 1

concepts.text: External Memory

A magnetic disk drive has one or more platters coated on both surfaces, each surface read by its own head on a common movable arm. Data lie on concentric tracks; each track is divided into sectors of typically 512 bytes or 4 KB, the smallest unit transferred. The set of tracks at the same radius on all surfaces is a cylinder, and a location is given by cylinder, head and sector. Reading a sector costs three delays: seek time, to move the head to the right track (a few ms); rotational latency, waiting for the sector to rotate under the head (on average half a revolution, 4.17 ms at 7200 rpm); and transfer time, proportional to the number of bytes and the rotation speed. Disks are block devices with direct (random) access, unlike tape, which is sequential.

concepts.plainText: T_access = T_seek + 1/(2r) + b/(rN), r = revolutions per second, b = bytes transferred, N = bytes per track

rows: 2; highest throughput, any disk failure loses all data
2; fast reads, tolerates one failure per mirrored pair
Block-level striping with parity distributed over all disks
3; tolerates one failure, small writes pay a read-modify-write parity penalty

concepts.text: Other external storage technologies:
items: Solid-state drive (SSD): NAND flash with a controller; no moving parts, so no seek or rotational delay (access in tens of μs), shock resistant and low power. Flash blocks must be erased before rewriting and wear out after roughly 10^4 to 10^5 program/erase cycles, so the controller does wear levelling and garbage collection.

Optical disc: data stored as pits and lands read by a laser along a single spiral track; CD about 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB per layer, Blu-ray 25 GB per layer; CD-ROM uses constant linear velocity (rotation speed changes with radius). Variants: read-only (pressed), recordable (-R, write once), rewritable (-RW).

Magnetic tape: sequential access on a long ribbon, serpentine recording of many parallel tracks; very high capacity per cartridge (LTO) and the lowest cost per bit, but access times of seconds to minutes, so it is used for backup and archive.
Access-time model for a non-random-access device: T_N = T_A + n/R, where T_A is the average time to reach the start, n the number of bits and R the transfer rate in bits per second.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Storage Timing, RAID and Virtual Memory

A memory hierarchy is judged by two averages. If level 1 holds S1 bits at a cost of C1 per bit and level 2 holds S2 bits at C2 per bit, the average cost per bit of the system is weighted by size, so a small expensive level hardly changes it when S1 is much smaller than S2. The access efficiency T1/Ts compares the access time of the fast level with the average access time the processor actually sees; it approaches 1 only when level 1 satisfies almost every reference, because a reference that goes to disk is many thousands of times slower. Together the two numbers state the goal of the hierarchy: speed close to T1 at a cost close to C2.

concepts.latex: C_s = \frac{C_1 S_1 + C_2 S_2}{S_1 + S_2},\quad E = \frac{T_1}{T_s}
concepts.plainText: Average cost per bit C_s = (C1 × S1 + C2 × S2) / (S1 + S2); access efficiency E = T1 / Ts, where Ts is the average access time seen by the processor

concepts.text: Disk capacity is the product of recording surfaces, tracks per surface, sectors per track and bytes per sector; a double-sided platter contributes two surfaces, and the number of cylinders equals the number of tracks per surface. Older drives use constant angular velocity (CAV) with the same number of sectors on every track, so the longer outer tracks are recorded at a lower bit density; modern drives use multiple-zone recording and put more sectors on the outer zones. Because one whole track passes under the head in every revolution, the sustained transfer rate equals the bytes per track multiplied by the revolutions per second (rpm / 60). A file stored on adjacent tracks pays the seek only once, while scattered sectors pay a seek and a rotational latency each, which is why disk layout matters so much.

Worked example 1: sequential versus random reading
Disk: average seek 8 ms, 6000 rpm, 250 sectors of 512 B per track
Revolution = 60 / 6000 s = 10 ms, average latency = 5 ms
One sector passes the head in 10 / 250 = 0.04 ms
File of 1000 sectors on 4 adjacent full tracks:
  track 1:     8 + 5 + 10 = 23 ms
  tracks 2-4:  3 x (5 + 10) = 45 ms   (track-to-track seek ignored)
  total      = 68 ms
Same 1000 sectors scattered at random:
  per sector:  8 + 5 + 0.04 = 13.04 ms
  total      = 1000 x 13.04 ms = 13.04 s (about 192 times slower)

rows: Usable capacity (n disks of size C)
Mirroring: every block written to two disks
Bit striping with Hamming-code check disks
(n − m)C, m check disks growing with log2 of the data disks
Byte or bit striping, one dedicated parity disk
Block striping, one dedicated parity disk
Block striping, parity rotated over all disks
Block striping, two independent check blocks P and Q

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: RAID 5 parity (one byte per block, hex)
Stripe: D0 = B2, D1 = 6C, D2 = 1F
Parity P = D0 xor D1 xor D2 = B2 xor 6C xor 1F = DE xor 1F = C1
Disk holding D1 fails, rebuild it from the survivors:
  D1 = P xor D0 xor D2 = C1 xor B2 xor 1F = 73 xor 1F = 6C
Small write, D2 changes from 1F to 20 (read-modify-write):
  read old D2 and old P                    2 reads
  P' = P xor D2old xor D2new = C1 xor 1F xor 20 = FE
  write new D2 and new P'                  2 writes
  total = 4 disk accesses for one small write
Check: B2 xor 6C xor 20 = FE
Details of semiconductor and optical storage that calculations rely on:
items: DRAM refresh overhead: with R rows, a retention period T_ref and a time t_r per row refresh, the fraction of time lost is R × t_r / T_ref. Burst refresh does all rows back to back; distributed refresh issues one row refresh every T_ref / R, for example 64 ms / 4096 rows = 15.6 µs.

NOR flash connects cells in parallel, giving random byte reads and execute-in-place for firmware; NAND flash connects cells in series strings, giving higher density with page reads and writes and block erase, the medium of SSDs and memory cards.

A flash cell storing n bits must distinguish 2^n charge levels: SLC 1 bit (2 levels), MLC 2 bits (4), TLC 3 bits (8), QLC 4 bits (16). More bits per cell lower the cost per bit but also the endurance and the write speed.

An SSD cannot overwrite a page in place: it writes the new data to an erased page, marks the old page invalid and later garbage-collects whole blocks; wear levelling spreads the program/erase cycles evenly over all blocks.

Optical discs record along one spiral track at constant linear velocity (CLV), so the drive spins faster near the centre. The laser wavelength limits the pit size: CD 780 nm (about 700 MB), DVD 650 nm (4.7 GB per layer), Blu-ray 405 nm (25 GB per layer).

concepts.text: Virtual memory adds one more level below main memory, which then acts as a cache for pages kept on disk or SSD. A virtual address is split into a virtual page number and an offset; the page table, indexed by the page number, supplies the physical frame number, and the offset is copied unchanged, so physical address = frame × page size + offset. If the entry is marked not present, a page fault traps to the operating system, which loads the page (replacing another one if memory is full) and restarts the instruction. Every translation would otherwise cost an extra memory access to read the page table, so recent translations are cached in a translation lookaside buffer (TLB).

concepts.plainText: EAT = (1 − p) × t_m + p × t_fault, where p = page-fault rate, t_m = memory access time and t_fault = page-fault service time

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: paging arithmetic
32-bit virtual address, 8 KB pages, 4-byte page-table entries
  offset = log2 8192 = 13 bits, page number = 32 - 13 = 19 bits
  page table = 2^19 entries x 4 B = 2 MB per process
Translate VA 0000 5A3C (hex); the table maps page 2 to frame 7
  page = 5A3C >> 13 = 2, offset = 5A3C - 4000 = 1A3C
  PA = 7 x 2000 + 1A3C = E000 + 1A3C = 0000 FA3C (hex)
Page faults: t_m = 60 ns, t_fault = 5 ms, p = 2 x 10^-6
  EAT = (1 - p) x 60 + p x 5,000,000 = 59.99988 + 10 = about 70 ns
TLB: lookup 5 ns, hit ratio 0.95, one-level page table
  EAT = 0.95 x (5 + 60) + 0.05 x (5 + 60 + 60) = 61.75 + 6.25 = 68 ns

Common slips in storage calculations: using rpm as revolutions per second (divide by 60 first); taking a full revolution instead of half of one as the average rotational latency; forgetting that a double-sided platter has two surfaces; mixing bits with bytes or 10^9 with 2^30; quoting the RAID 1 capacity as the sum of both disks; charging the average seek to every track of a file stored on adjacent tracks; and writing 8 ms as 8,000 ns in page-fault problems (it is 8,000,000 ns).

formulas.plainText: Two-level hierarchy: T_avg = h × T_1 + (1 − h) × T_2, where h is the hit ratio of the fast level
Average rotational latency = half a revolution = 30 / rpm seconds (4.17 ms at 7200 rpm)
Disk access time = seek + average rotational latency + transfer time b/(rN)
Hamming SEC code: k check bits for m data bits need 2^k ≥ m + k + 1
Memory capacity = 2^n words × w bits per word, n = address lines

notes.text: Going down the hierarchy (registers → cache → main memory → disk → tape) four things change together: access time up, capacity up, cost per bit down, access frequency down. MCQs often ask which of these is the odd one out.

Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile. The difference is refresh: DRAM stores charge on a capacitor and must be refreshed every few milliseconds; SRAM stores the bit in a flip-flop and needs no refresh but uses about six transistors per cell, which is why it is used only for cache.
RAID 0 gives speed but no redundancy; RAID 1 gives redundancy by mirroring at 50% overhead; RAID 5 spreads parity so that n disks give (n − 1) disks of usable space and survive one failure.
Rotational latency questions: average latency is half a revolution. 7200 rpm = 120 rev/s → 8.33 ms per revolution → 4.17 ms average; 5400 rpm → 5.56 ms; 10000 rpm → 3 ms.

formulas.description: Effective access time of a two-level hierarchy with hit ratio h in the fast level; the same form gives cache-plus-main-memory or main-memory-plus-disk figures.

formulas.plainText: T_access = T_seek + 1/(2r) + b/(rN)
formulas.description: Seek time plus average rotational latency (half a revolution at r rev/s) plus the transfer time of b bytes from a track holding N bytes.

formulas.title: Average rotational latency
formulas.plainText: T_rot = 30 / rpm seconds
formulas.description: Half of one revolution period; 7200 rpm gives 4.17 ms, 5400 rpm gives 5.56 ms, 15000 rpm gives 2 ms.

formulas.title: Hamming check bits
