flashcards.front: State the two kinds of locality of reference and give an example of each.
flashcards.back: Temporal: a recently used item is likely to be used again soon (loop variables). Spatial: items near a used address are likely to be used soon (sequential instructions, array traversal).

flashcards.front: Why does a DRAM chip need RAS and CAS signals?
flashcards.back: The address is multiplexed in two halves to halve the pin count: RAS latches the row address and CAS the column address into the chip's square cell array.

flashcards.front: How does flash differ from EEPROM?
flashcards.back: Both are electrically erasable and non-volatile, but EEPROM erases and writes byte by byte, whereas flash erases a whole block (sector) at a time, giving much higher density and faster bulk writes.

flashcards.front: What are the three components of magnetic disk access time?
flashcards.back: Seek time (move the head to the track), rotational latency (wait for the sector; average half a revolution) and transfer time (proportional to bytes read and rotation speed).

questions.questionText: A hard disk rotates at 7200 rpm. Its average rotational latency is approximately:
questions.explanation: 7200 rpm is 120 revolutions per second, so one revolution takes 8.33 ms. The average wait is half a revolution, 4.17 ms.

questions.questionText: The minimum number of check bits required by a Hamming single-error-correcting code for 16 data bits is:
questions.explanation: The condition is 2^k ≥ m + k + 1. For m = 16, k = 4 gives 16 < 21 (fails) and k = 5 gives 32 ≥ 22, so 5 check bits are needed.

questions.questionText: Moving down the memory hierarchy from CPU registers towards magnetic tape, which of the following does NOT happen?
options: The frequency of access by the processor increases
questions.explanation: Going down the hierarchy the access time and capacity rise and the cost per bit falls, while the processor accesses the lower levels less often, not more. That falling access frequency is what lets the small fast levels serve most references.

questions.questionText: A loop counter i is read and updated in every iteration of a loop. Keeping i in a register or in the cache after its first use exploits which property of programs?
questions.explanation: Temporal locality means that a location referenced now is likely to be referenced again soon; the repeated use of the same variable i is the classic example. Spatial and sequential locality concern neighbouring addresses such as successive array elements or instructions.

questions.questionText: A two-level storage system has 1 GB of level-1 memory costing $10 per GB and 99 GB of level-2 memory costing $0.10 per GB. What is the average cost per GB of the whole system?
questions.explanation: Average cost C_s = (C1 S1 + C2 S2) / (S1 + S2) = (10 × 1 + 0.10 × 99) / (1 + 99) = 19.9 / 100 = $0.199 per GB, close to the price of the large cheap level. Averaging the two prices ($5.05) ignores the sizes of the levels.

questions.questionText: A single dynamic RAM (DRAM) storage cell consists of:
options: A cross-coupled flip-flop of about six transistors
A floating-gate transistor that traps charge
A fusible link that is blown during programming
questions.explanation: A DRAM cell stores the bit as charge on a capacitor reached through one access transistor, which makes it dense and cheap but forces periodic refresh. Six-transistor flip-flops are SRAM cells, floating gates are EPROM/flash cells and fuses are PROM cells.

questions.questionText: Which statement about SRAM and DRAM is NOT correct?
options: SRAM needs periodic refresh because the charge in its flip-flop slowly leaks away
DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit because each cell needs only one transistor and one capacitor
Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile
SRAM is faster than DRAM, which is why it is used for cache memory
questions.explanation: SRAM keeps each bit in a bistable flip-flop that holds its state as long as power is applied, so it needs no refresh. It is DRAM whose capacitor charge leaks and must be refreshed every few milliseconds; the other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: Why is the cycle time of a DRAM longer than its access time?
options: The DRAM must wait for the next refresh period after every access
The data must pass through an ECC circuit before they can be sent to the processor
The column address can be decoded only after the data of the previous access have been removed from the bus
A read discharges the cells of the selected row, so the row must be restored and the bit lines precharged before the next access can begin
questions.explanation: Access time is the delay from address to data out, whereas cycle time is the minimum interval between the starts of two accesses. The DRAM read is destructive, so the sense amplifiers write the row back and the bit lines are precharged after the data appear, which makes the cycle time exceed the access time.

questions.questionText: A 256M × 1 DRAM chip multiplexes its row and column addresses over the same pins using RAS and CAS, with equal numbers of row and column address bits. How many address pins does it need?
questions.explanation: 256M = 2^28 cells need a 28-bit address. With 2^14 rows × 2^14 columns, the 14-bit row address is latched by RAS and then the 14-bit column address by CAS over the same 14 pins, halving the pin count.

questions.questionText: A DDR SDRAM module has a 64-bit data bus and a 200 MHz bus clock. What is its peak transfer rate? (1 GB/s = 10^9 bytes per second)
questions.explanation: DDR moves data on both clock edges: 200 × 10^6 × 2 transfers/s × 8 bytes = 3.2 × 10^9 bytes/s = 3.2 GB/s (the DDR-400 or PC-3200 rating). Ignoring the double data rate gives 1.6 GB/s, and 25.6 is the figure in gigabits per second.

questions.questionText: A DRAM has 8192 rows, each of which must be refreshed every 64 ms, and one row refresh keeps the chip busy for 50 ns. What fraction of the time is the DRAM busy refreshing, and what is the interval between row refreshes if they are spread evenly (distributed refresh)?
questions.explanation: Refresh work per period = 8192 × 50 ns = 409.6 µs, and 409.6 µs / 64 ms = 0.0064 = 0.64% of the time. Spread evenly, the rows are refreshed every 64 ms / 8192 = 7.8125 µs, about 7.8 µs.

questions.questionText: How is a conventional EPROM erased?
options: Electrically, one byte at a time, while the chip stays in the circuit
Electrically, one block at a time, by commands from the processor
By exposing the chip to ultraviolet light through its quartz window, which erases the whole chip
It cannot be erased, because its bit pattern is fixed by a photomask
questions.explanation: An EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light, typically for several minutes, and the entire chip is cleared at once. Electrical byte erase describes EEPROM, electrical block erase describes flash, and a fixed photomask describes mask ROM.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes flash memory from EEPROM?
options: Flash is erased electrically a whole block at a time, whereas EEPROM can be erased and rewritten a byte at a time
Flash is erased by ultraviolet light, whereas EEPROM is erased electrically
Flash is volatile, whereas EEPROM is non-volatile
Flash can be programmed only once, whereas EEPROM can be rewritten many times
questions.explanation: Both are electrically erasable and non-volatile. Flash gives up byte-level erasure in exchange for a smaller, denser cell and erases a block (sector) at a time, which is why it replaced EEPROM for bulk storage.

questions.questionText: Which statement about NOR and NAND flash is correct?
options: NOR flash allows random byte reads and execute-in-place, so it suits program code; NAND flash is denser and is read and written in pages, so it suits bulk storage such as SSDs
NAND flash allows execute-in-place and random byte reads, while NOR flash is used in SSDs because it is denser
NOR and NAND flash differ only in their supply voltage
NAND flash can be erased one byte at a time, whereas NOR flash can only be erased as a whole chip
questions.explanation: NOR cells sit in parallel on the bit lines, giving fast random reads so the processor can execute firmware directly from the chip. NAND cells form series strings, giving a smaller cell and higher density, with page reads and writes and block erase, which makes NAND the medium for SSDs, USB drives and memory cards.

questions.questionText: Which of the following memories retains its contents when the power is removed?
questions.explanation: Flash stores charge on an insulated floating gate that stays for years without power, so it is non-volatile. SRAM, DRAM and SDRAM (a synchronous DRAM) all lose their contents when power is removed.

questions.questionText: A QLC NAND flash cell stores 4 bits. How many distinct charge (threshold-voltage) levels must the cell be able to hold and distinguish?
questions.explanation: n bits per cell need 2^n distinguishable levels: SLC 2, MLC 4, TLC 8 and QLC 2^4 = 16. More levels raise the density but shrink the margin between levels, which lowers endurance and speed.

questions.questionText: An SSD controller receives a request to overwrite a logical page that already holds data. What normally happens?
options: The page is erased and rewritten in place, because flash can be erased one page at a time
The new data are written to a free, already erased page, the old page is marked invalid, and garbage collection later erases whole blocks to reclaim space
The whole SSD is erased and then rewritten with the new data
The data are kept only in the SSD's DRAM cache and never reach the flash
questions.explanation: Flash cannot be rewritten in place: a page must be erased before it is programmed again, and erasure works only on whole blocks of many pages. The controller therefore maps the logical page to a fresh physical page and reclaims stale pages later, while wear levelling spreads the writes evenly.

questions.questionText: A byte is stored with a 12-bit Hamming SEC code whose check bits occupy bit positions 1, 2, 4 and 8. On a read, the syndrome C8 C4 C2 C1 is 0101. Assuming at most one bit is in error, which statement is correct?
options: Check bits C4 and C1 are both in error
Bit position 5, which holds a data bit, is in error and is corrected by inverting it
Bit position 10, which holds a data bit, is in error
There is no error, because the syndrome contains an even number of 1s
questions.explanation: Read as a binary number, the syndrome is the position of the flipped bit: 0101 = 5. Position 5 is not a power of two, so it is a data bit, and inverting it restores the word; reading the syndrome in reverse bit order would wrongly give 1010 = 10.

questions.questionText: An ECC memory module protects each 64-bit data word with a SEC-DED (single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting) Hamming code. How many bits are stored per word?
questions.explanation: SEC needs k check bits with 2^k ≥ 64 + k + 1: k = 6 gives 64 < 71 (fails) and k = 7 gives 128 ≥ 72. One more overall parity bit adds double-error detection, so 64 + 7 + 1 = 72 bits are stored; 71 bits would give SEC only.

questions.questionText: On a multi-platter magnetic disk, the set of tracks that lie at the same radius on all recording surfaces is called a:
questions.explanation: All heads move together on one arm, so the tracks under them at one arm position form a cylinder and can be read without another seek. A sector is part of one track, a cluster is a file-system allocation unit, and a zone is a band of adjacent tracks in multiple-zone recording.

questions.questionText: A server disk spins at 15,000 rpm. What is its average rotational latency?
questions.explanation: 15,000 rpm = 250 revolutions per second, so one revolution takes 1/250 s = 4 ms. On average the wanted sector is half a revolution away: 4 / 2 = 2 ms.

questions.questionText: A disk drive has 4 platters, both surfaces of each used for data, with 20,000 tracks per surface, 500 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector. What is its capacity? (1 GB = 10^9 bytes)
questions.explanation: Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector = 8 × 20,000 × 500 × 512 = 40,960,000,000 bytes = 40.96 GB. Counting only 4 surfaces gives 20.48 GB.

questions.questionText: A disk has an average seek time of 4 ms, rotates at 10,000 rpm and has 500 sectors per track. What is the average time to read one randomly located sector? (Ignore controller overhead.)
questions.explanation: One revolution takes 60 / 10,000 s = 6 ms, so the average rotational latency is 3 ms and one sector passes the head in 6 / 500 = 0.012 ms. T = 4 + 3 + 0.012 = 7.012 ms; using a full revolution as the latency gives 10.012 ms.

questions.questionText: A disk spins at 12,000 rpm and every track holds 256 KB. What is its maximum sustained transfer rate when reading whole tracks? (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB)
questions.explanation: 12,000 rpm = 200 revolutions per second, and one full track passes the head in each revolution: 256 KB × 200 = 51,200 KB/s = 50 MB/s. Forgetting to divide the rpm by 60 gives 3000 MB/s, and 400 is the rate in megabits per second.

questions.questionText: A magnetic disk uses constant angular velocity (CAV) with the same number of sectors on every track. Which statement is correct?
options: Outer tracks hold more bits than inner tracks, so the transfer rate is higher on the outer tracks
The disk slows down whenever the head moves to the outer tracks
Outer tracks are longer but hold the same number of bits, so their bit density is lower and capacity is wasted; multiple-zone recording addresses this
The innermost tracks cannot be used because their bit density would be too high
questions.explanation: With CAV and equal sectors per track, a sector is easy to locate by track and sector number, but the outermost track stores no more than the innermost one. Multiple-zone recording divides the surface into zones and gives the outer zones more sectors per track to raise the capacity.

questions.questionText: A disk has 16 recording surfaces, 1024 tracks per surface, 256 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector, and rotates at 6000 rpm. What are its capacity and its maximum data transfer rate? (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB)
questions.explanation: Capacity = 16 × 1024 × 256 × 512 = 2^31 bytes = 2 GB. One track holds 256 × 512 B = 128 KB and passes the head 6000 / 60 = 100 times per second, so the rate is 12,800 KB/s = 12.5 MB/s; not dividing the rpm by 60 gives 750 MB/s.

questions.questionText: A disk has an average seek time of 5 ms, rotates at 10,000 rpm and has 400 sectors of 512 bytes per track. A file of 1600 sectors occupies 4 complete adjacent tracks. Assuming the track-to-track seek time is negligible and that each track needs an average rotational latency before reading starts, how long does it take to read the file sequentially?
questions.explanation: One revolution = 60 / 10,000 s = 6 ms, the average latency is 3 ms, and a full track is read in one revolution. First track: 5 + 3 + 6 = 14 ms; each of the other 3 tracks: 3 + 6 = 9 ms; total = 14 + 3 × 9 = 41 ms. Charging the full seek to every track gives 4 × 14 = 56 ms.

questions.questionText: A disk has an average seek time of 5 ms, rotates at 10,000 rpm and has 400 sectors per track. The 1600 sectors of a file are scattered at random over the disk, so every sector needs its own seek and rotational latency. How long does it take to read the whole file?
questions.explanation: Per sector: 5 ms seek + 3 ms average latency (half of 6 ms) + 6 / 400 = 0.015 ms transfer = 8.015 ms. For 1600 sectors: 1600 × 8.015 ms = 12,824 ms ≈ 12.82 s. Using a full revolution as the latency gives 17.62 s.

questions.questionText: Compared with a magnetic hard disk, which components of the access time are essentially absent in a solid-state drive (SSD)?
options: Rotational latency only; an SSD still has a seek time
Seek time only; an SSD still has a rotational latency
questions.explanation: An SSD has no moving arm and no spinning platters, so there is no mechanical seek and no wait for a sector to rotate under a head. Only the controller overhead, the flash read time and the transfer time remain.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes constant linear velocity (CLV) recording as used on a CD-ROM?
options: The disc spins at a constant rpm, so the outer part of the track holds fewer bits per millimetre
Data are recorded on concentric tracks that all have the same number of sectors
The spiral track passes the laser at a constant speed, so the disc spins faster when the head reads near the centre than near the outer edge
The laser head moves at a constant speed while the disc stays stationary
questions.explanation: With CLV the bit density is uniform along the single spiral track, which maximises the capacity. To keep the linear speed constant, the rotation rate must fall as the head moves outwards (roughly 500 rpm at the centre to 200 rpm at the edge for a 1× CD); constant rpm with lower outer density describes CAV.

questions.questionText: Why can a Blu-ray disc hold much more data per layer than a CD or a DVD of the same diameter?
options: It spins at constant angular velocity, so its outer tracks hold more data
It uses a shorter-wavelength (405 nm blue-violet) laser, which allows smaller pits and a narrower track pitch
It stores the data magnetically instead of as pits and lands
It records data on both surfaces of the disc at the same time
questions.explanation: The smallest spot a laser can be focused to scales with its wavelength (CD 780 nm, DVD 650 nm, Blu-ray 405 nm), and Blu-ray also uses a lens with a larger numerical aperture. Smaller pits on a tighter spiral raise the capacity from about 0.7 GB (CD) and 4.7 GB (DVD) to 25 GB per layer.

questions.questionText: Which storage medium offers only sequential access, so that the time to reach a record depends strongly on where it is stored?
questions.explanation: Tape must be wound past all the data in between to reach a record, which is sequential access. A disk gives direct access (seek to a track, then wait for the sector), and RAM gives random access with the same access time for every location.

questions.questionText: A tape drive needs on average 30 s to position the tape at the start of a file and then transfers data at 300 MB/s. How long does it take to read a 6 GB file? (1 GB = 1000 MB)
questions.explanation: For a sequential-access device T_N = T_A + n / R = 30 s + 6000 MB / (300 MB/s) = 30 + 20 = 50 s. Omitting the positioning time gives 20 s, and reading the rate as 300 Mbit/s gives 30 + 160 = 190 s.

questions.questionText: Which RAID level stripes data blocks across several disks but stores no redundant information at all?
questions.explanation: RAID 0 only stripes, giving high throughput and 100% usable capacity, but the failure of any one disk loses the data of the array. RAID 1 mirrors, and RAID 4 and RAID 5 add parity.

questions.questionText: Two 4 TB disks are configured as a RAID 1 mirrored pair. Which statement about the array is correct?
options: It provides 8 TB of usable space and survives the failure of either disk
It provides 4 TB of usable space and survives the failure of either disk
It provides 4 TB of usable space but cannot survive any disk failure
It provides 2 TB of usable space and survives the failure of both disks
questions.explanation: RAID 1 writes every block to both disks, so the usable space equals one disk: 2 × 4 TB / 2 = 4 TB. Because each disk holds a complete copy, the array keeps working if either disk fails.

questions.questionText: Which RAID level uses block-level striping with all parity blocks on one dedicated disk, so that this parity disk becomes a bottleneck when many small writes occur?
questions.explanation: RAID 4 uses large (block) strips and a single parity disk that every write must update, so small writes queue up on it. RAID 5 removes the bottleneck by rotating the parity over all disks, and RAID 3 uses bit- or byte-level strips with parallel access.

questions.questionText: Which RAID level stripes data at the bit level and uses a Hamming code, stored on several check disks, to correct errors?
questions.explanation: RAID 2 spreads very small strips over synchronised disks and computes a Hamming code across corresponding bits, which needs several check disks. Since drives already have internal error correction it is not used in practice; RAID 3 needs only a single parity disk.

questions.questionText: Five 2 TB disks form a RAID 5 array. What is its usable capacity, and how many simultaneous disk failures can it survive?
questions.explanation: RAID 5 uses one disk's worth of space for distributed parity: (5 − 1) × 2 TB = 8 TB. The parity can rebuild any single failed disk, but a second failure before the rebuild finishes loses data; 6 TB with two-failure tolerance would be RAID 6.

questions.questionText: Six 4 TB disks are configured as RAID 6. What is the usable capacity?
questions.explanation: RAID 6 keeps two independent check blocks (P and Q) in every stripe, which costs two disks' worth of space: (6 − 2) × 4 TB = 16 TB. In return it survives any two simultaneous disk failures; 20 TB would be RAID 5 and 24 TB RAID 0.

questions.questionText: An array is to be built from four identical disks and must survive the failure of any one disk. Which RAID level gives the largest usable capacity?
questions.explanation: With 4 disks RAID 5 keeps 3 disks of data (75%), while mirrored pairs (RAID 10) and RAID 6 keep only 2 disks of data (50%). RAID 0 keeps all 4 disks but cannot survive any failure, so it does not meet the requirement.

questions.questionText: In a RAID 5 stripe the data blocks and the parity block hold (one byte of each shown, in hexadecimal) D0 = 5A, D1 = 3C, D2 = F0 and P = 96. The application overwrites D1 with 0F. Using the read-modify-write method, what is the new parity byte and how many disk accesses does this small write need?
options: A5; 2 accesses (write new D1 and new P)
A5; 4 accesses (read old D1 and old P, then write new D1 and new P)
99; 4 accesses (read old D1 and old P, then write new D1 and new P)
33; 3 accesses (read old D1, then write new D1 and new P)
questions.explanation: P_new = P_old ⊕ D1_old ⊕ D1_new = 96 ⊕ 3C ⊕ 0F = AA ⊕ 0F = A5, which matches 5A ⊕ 0F ⊕ F0 = A5. The old data and old parity must be read before the new data and parity are written, so one small write costs 2 reads + 2 writes = 4 accesses.

questions.questionText: In a virtual memory system, a page fault occurs when:
options: The required block is not in the cache and must be fetched from main memory
The TLB has no entry for the page, although the page is in main memory
Two processes try to access the same physical frame at the same time
The referenced page is not in main memory, so it must be brought in from secondary storage
questions.explanation: A page fault is raised when the page-table entry shows that the page is not resident; the operating system then loads it from disk or SSD. A cache miss and a TLB miss are far cheaper events that need no transfer from secondary storage.

questions.questionText: The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is best described as:
options: A buffer that holds dirty cache lines until they are written back to main memory
The area of the disk that holds pages swapped out of main memory
A register that holds the starting address of the page table
A small, fast cache of recently used page-table entries that speeds up virtual-to-physical address translation
questions.explanation: Without a TLB every memory reference would need an extra memory access to read the page table; the TLB keeps recent translations so most references are translated almost instantly. The swap area and the page-table base register are separate structures.

questions.questionText: A system uses 1 KB pages (1 KB = 1024 bytes) and byte addresses. Virtual page 4 of a process is mapped to physical frame 9. Which physical address corresponds to virtual address 5000 (decimal)?
questions.explanation: Page number = 5000 div 1024 = 4 and offset = 5000 − 4 × 1024 = 904. Page 4 is in frame 9, so the physical address = 9 × 1024 + 904 = 9216 + 904 = 10120.

questions.questionText: A system has 32-bit virtual byte addresses, 4 KB pages (1 KB = 1024 bytes) and a single-level page table with 4-byte entries. How many bits form the virtual page number, and how large is the full page table of one process?
questions.explanation: The offset is log2(4096) = 12 bits, so the page number has 32 − 12 = 20 bits and the table has 2^20 entries. Its size is 2^20 × 4 bytes = 4 MB (1 MB = 1024 KB); forgetting the 4-byte entry size gives 1 MB.

questions.questionText: Main memory access time is 100 ns and servicing a page fault takes 8 ms. If one memory access in 100,000 causes a page fault, what is the effective access time, using EAT = (1 − p) × memory access time + p × page-fault service time? (Ignore TLB and cache effects.)
questions.explanation: EAT = (1 − p) × 100 ns + p × 8 ms with p = 10^-5: 0.99999 × 100 + 10^-5 × 8,000,000 ns = 99.999 + 80 ≈ 180 ns. Even such rare faults slow memory by about 80%, because each costs 80,000 normal accesses; writing 8 ms as 8,000 ns gives the 100.08 ns distractor.

questions.questionText: Main memory access time is 200 ns, a page fault takes 10 ms to service, and EAT = (1 − p) × 200 ns + p × 10 ms, where p is the page-fault rate. To keep the slowdown caused by page faults below 5% (EAT below 210 ns), p must be below about:
questions.explanation: Require (1 − p) × 200 + p × 10,000,000 < 210 ns, so p × 9,999,800 < 10 and p < 1.0 × 10^-6: at most about one fault per 1,000,000 accesses. Writing 10 ms as 1,000,000 ns gives the 1-in-100,000 distractor.

questions.questionText: A paged system has a TLB with a lookup time of 10 ns and a hit ratio of 90%, a main-memory access time of 100 ns and a single-level page table held in main memory. The TLB is searched first; on a TLB miss the page-table entry is read from memory before the data access. Ignoring page faults and caches, what is the effective memory access time?
questions.explanation: TLB hit: 10 + 100 = 110 ns; TLB miss: 10 + 100 (page-table entry) + 100 (data) = 210 ns. EAT = 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns, compared with 200 ns if there were no TLB at all.

subtopics.title: Cache Memory Principles & Design
subtopics.subtitle: Hit ratio, access time, cache mapping with bit splits, replacement and write policies

concepts.text: Why Cache Works

A cache is a small, fast SRAM placed between the processor and main memory that holds copies of the main-memory blocks most recently used. Main memory is viewed as 2^n / K blocks of K words; the cache has m lines, each holding one block plus a tag that identifies which block it is and a valid bit. On every reference the processor first looks in the cache: a hit delivers the word immediately; a miss makes the cache fetch the whole block containing the word from main memory into a line (exploiting spatial locality) and then deliver the word. Because of temporal and spatial locality most references hit, so the processor sees nearly cache speed with main-memory capacity. The cache is transparent: programs need no changes.

concepts.plainText: t_avg = h × t_c + (1 − h) × t_m, h = hit ratio, t_c = cache access time, t_m = main-memory access time

concepts.text: Worked example: t_c = 10 ns, t_m = 100 ns, h = 0.9. Then t_avg = 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 9 + 10 = 19 ns, and the speed-up over memory alone is 100 / 19 ≈ 5.3. If the question states that main memory is accessed only after the cache lookup fails (look-through with no overlap), the miss cost is t_c + t_m and t_avg = 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 20 ns. The hit ratio h is hits divided by total references; the miss ratio is 1 − h, and the miss penalty is the extra time a miss costs.
Cache size is the first design element and is a trade-off:
items: A larger cache raises the hit ratio, but with diminishing returns once the working set of the program fits.
A larger cache is slower (bigger tag comparison and addressing logic), costs more and takes chip area; the cost per bit should stay close to that of main memory overall.
Typical sizes: L1 16–64 KB per core, L2 256 KB to a few MB, L3 several MB to tens of MB shared by all cores.

Cache performance is also limited by compulsory misses (first touch), capacity misses (working set larger than cache) and conflict misses (blocks competing for the same line), which the mapping function influences.

concepts.text: Mapping Functions

The mapping function decides which cache line a main-memory block may occupy, and it fixes how the memory address is split into fields. Running example for all three mappings: a byte-addressable main memory of 64 KB (16-bit address), a cache of 2 KB and a block (line) size of 16 bytes. The cache therefore has 2048 / 16 = 128 lines, main memory has 4096 blocks, and the lowest 4 address bits (the word or byte-offset field) select a byte within a block in every mapping.
Direct mapping: block j goes to line i = j mod m (m = number of lines):
items: Address fields: tag | line | word. Line field = log2(128) = 7 bits, word = 4 bits, tag = 16 − 7 − 4 = 5 bits. Each line can hold any of 2^5 = 32 different blocks, distinguished by the tag stored with it.
Access: use the line bits to select one line, compare its stored tag with the tag bits of the address, and check the valid bit. Only one comparator is needed, so it is simple, fast and cheap.

Weakness: two frequently used blocks that map to the same line keep evicting each other (thrashing, conflict misses) even when the rest of the cache is empty. No replacement algorithm is needed because there is no choice.
Example: block 0, block 128 and block 256 all map to line 0; block 5 maps to line 5 with tag 0, block 133 maps to line 5 with tag 1.

concepts.text: Fully associative mapping: a block can be loaded into any line:
items: Address fields: tag | word. Tag = 16 − 4 = 12 bits, which is the full block number; there is no line field.

Access: the tag of the address must be compared with the tags of all 128 lines simultaneously, which needs one comparator per line or a content-addressable (associative) memory. This is expensive and limits the size.
Strength: no conflict misses; a block is evicted only when the cache is full, so a replacement algorithm is essential.
Used where the cache is small, for example translation lookaside buffers and some L1 caches.

concepts.text: Set-associative mapping: the cache is divided into v sets of k lines each (k-way), and block j goes to set i = j mod v:
items: Address fields: tag | set | word. In the example a 2-way cache has 128 / 2 = 64 sets, so set = 6 bits and tag = 16 − 6 − 4 = 6 bits; a 4-way cache has 32 sets, set = 5 bits and tag = 7 bits.
Access: the set bits select one set, then the k tags of that set are compared in parallel, so only k comparators are needed.

k = 1 is direct mapping and k = m is fully associative; 2-way to 8-way is the usual compromise, giving most of the hit-ratio benefit of full associativity at modest cost. Replacement is needed within a set.
Increasing k from 1 to 2 gives the largest hit-ratio gain; beyond 8-way the improvement is small.

concepts.plainText: tag bits = address bits − set (or line) bits − word bits; sets = lines / k, lines = cache size / block size

rows: the k lines of one set

concepts.text: Replacement Algorithms and Write Policies
When a new block must be loaded into a full set (associative or set-associative caches; direct mapping has no choice) a hardware replacement algorithm picks the victim:
items: LRU (least recently used): replace the block that has gone unreferenced for the longest time; best approximation of the optimal policy and the most used. A 2-way set needs only one USE bit per pair; larger sets keep age counters or use approximations such as pseudo-LRU.
FIFO (first-in first-out): replace the block that has been in the set longest, regardless of use; implemented with a round-robin pointer; may evict a heavily used block.
LFU (least frequently used): replace the block with the fewest references; needs a counter per line and unfairly penalises a block just loaded.
Random: pick any line; simplest hardware and in simulation only slightly worse than LRU.

concepts.text: Write policy decides how a write to a cached block reaches main memory:
items: Write-through: every write updates both the cache and main memory, so memory is always current (safe for I/O modules and other processors that read memory directly) but memory traffic is high. A write buffer between cache and memory lets the processor continue while the memory write completes.

Write-back: a write updates only the cache and sets the line's dirty (update) bit; the block is written to main memory only when it is evicted and its dirty bit is set. Traffic is much lower, but memory can be stale, so I/O and multiprocessor accesses must go through the cache or the cache must be flushed.

Write miss handling: write-allocate loads the block into the cache and then writes (natural with write-back); no-write-allocate (write-around) writes directly to memory without loading the block (natural with write-through).
Typical combination: write-through with a write buffer for L1, write-back for L2/L3.

concepts.text: Line Size, Number of Caches and Coherence
The remaining elements of cache design:
items: Line (block) size: larger lines bring in more neighbouring words and raise the hit ratio at first (spatial locality), but with a fixed cache size fewer lines fit, useful data get replaced sooner and each miss takes longer to service; the hit ratio rises then falls, with 32–128 bytes being typical.

Number of caches, levels: a multilevel hierarchy places a small, very fast L1 on the core, a larger L2 on the chip and an L3 shared by all cores; each level is checked in turn and the average access time nests as t_avg = h1·t1 + (1 − h1)[h2·t2 + (1 − h2)·t_m].

Number of caches, unified vs split: a unified cache holds instructions and data together and balances itself automatically, giving a higher hit ratio for a given size; a split (Harvard-style) cache has separate instruction and data caches so that instruction fetch and data access in a pipeline never contend for the same cache. Modern processors use a split L1 and unified L2/L3.
Cache and virtual memory: a cache can be addressed by physical or virtual addresses; a physically addressed cache needs the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) lookup first.

concepts.text: Cache coherence is the problem of keeping multiple copies of the same block consistent. It arises in a multiprocessor where each processor has its own cache, and with DMA devices that write main memory directly. With write-back caches a processor can hold a modified copy that other processors and main memory do not see; even with write-through, another cache may still hold an old copy. Solutions include bus watching (snooping) with write-through, in which every cache monitors the bus and invalidates its copy when it sees a write to that block; hardware directory protocols that record which caches hold each block; snoopy protocols such as MESI that mark each line Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid; and marking shared data as non-cacheable. This topic is expanded in the multiprocessor section of 4.3.
Going Deeper: Address Decoding, Traces and Cache Cost

Every mapping problem reduces to the same three steps. First find the block number, which is the address divided by the block size (drop the word field). Then find the index: block mod number of lines for direct mapping, or block mod number of sets for set-associative mapping; the remaining high-order part, block div number of sets, is the tag. When the address is given in hexadecimal it is quicker to write out the bits and cut them into fields from the right: word bits first, then index bits, and the rest is the tag.

Worked example 1: splitting an address
32-bit byte address, 64 KB cache, 32-byte blocks (1 KB = 1024 B)
lines = 65536 / 32 = 2048, word field = log2 32 = 5 bits
Direct mapped: line = log2 2048 = 11 bits, tag = 32 - 11 - 5 = 16 bits
4-way:  sets = 2048 / 4 = 512, set = 9 bits, tag = 32 - 9 - 5 = 18 bits
Address 7F3A5B64 (hex), block = address >> 5 = 03F9D2DB
  direct: line = block mod 2048 = 2DB (731), tag = 7F3A, word = 04
  4-way:  set = block mod 512 = 0DB (219), tag = 1FCE9, word = 04
Storage of the direct-mapped version if write-back (valid + dirty bit):
  2048 x (256 data + 16 tag + 2 status) = 561,152 bits = 68.5 KB

The capacity quoted for a cache, such as 64 KB, counts only the data. Every line also stores its tag, a valid bit, a dirty bit if the cache is write-back and, in set-associative caches, replacement state such as LRU bits. Each doubling of associativity lengthens every tag by one bit, so a fully associative cache has the largest tag store. Multiply the bits per line by the number of lines, and divide by 8 when the answer is wanted in bytes.

concepts.plainText: Total cache bits = m × (8K + t + v + d): m lines, K bytes per block, t tag bits, v valid bits and d dirty bits per line (add replacement bits if the question includes them)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: LRU versus FIFO in a 2-way cache
2 sets of 2 lines, set = block mod 2, cache initially empty
Contents of the set used, least recent (LRU) or oldest (FIFO) first
block set  LRU    result        FIFO   result

  4    0   [2 4]  miss, 6 out   [6 4]  miss, 2 out
  5    1   [5]    miss          [5]    miss

  4    0   [2 4]  hit           [4 2]  hit

LRU: 4 hits, 6 misses        FIFO: 2 hits, 8 misses

rows: Working set larger than the whole cache
Too many active blocks map to the same line or set
Another processor's write invalidated the copy

concepts.text: Architecture texts usually write the average access time as AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, which is the hierarchical (look-through) model: the cache is always probed and a miss adds the penalty. The penalty itself is the time to fetch a block, the memory latency plus the block size divided by the bus bandwidth, so larger blocks raise it. For a processor, memory stalls add to the base CPI: stall cycles per instruction = memory references per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty. With two levels, the L1 miss penalty is the AMAT of L2, and the product of the L1 miss rate and the L2 local miss rate is the global miss rate that reaches main memory.

concepts.plainText: AMAT = t1 + m1 × (t2 + m2 × t_mem), where t1, t2 are the L1 and L2 hit times, m1 the L1 miss rate and m2 the L2 local miss rate

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: two-level cache and CPI
L1: hit time 1 cycle, miss rate 5%
L2: hit time 12 cycles, local miss rate 30%; memory 120 cycles
L1 miss penalty = 12 + 0.30 x 120 = 48 cycles
AMAT = 1 + 0.05 x 48 = 3.4 cycles   (without L2: 1 + 0.05 x 120 = 7)
Global miss rate = 0.05 x 0.30 = 1.5% of references reach memory
Base CPI 1.0, 1.3 memory references per instruction:
  stall cycles per instruction = 1.3 x 0.05 x 48 = 3.12
  CPI = 1.0 + 3.12 = 4.12
Mistakes that cost marks in cache problems:
items: Mixing the two access-time models: the simultaneous form h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m and the look-through form t_c + (1 − h)·t_m differ by (1 − h)·t_c, so always state which one is used.
Using log2 of the cache size in bytes instead of log2 of the number of lines (or sets) as the index field.
Taking the block size in bits instead of bytes, or assuming byte addressing when the memory is word-addressable.
Forgetting that the tag grows by one bit each time the associativity doubles, and that a fully associative cache has no index field at all.
Counting only the data bits when the total cache size is asked; tags, valid, dirty and LRU bits are storage too.
In traces, mapping the address instead of the block number: divide by the block size first, then take the block number mod the number of sets.

concepts.text: For hit/miss traces draw one column per set and keep its blocks in order, least recently used (LRU) or oldest (FIFO) on the left. On a hit, LRU moves the block to the right end while FIFO changes nothing; on a miss in a full set, both remove the leftmost block and append the new one on the right.

formulas.plainText: Average access time t_avg = h × t_c + (1 − h) × t_m
Look-through form when memory is accessed only after a cache miss: t_avg = t_c + (1 − h) × t_m
Lines m = cache size C / block size K; sets v = m / k for a k-way cache
Tag bits = address bits − set bits (log2 v) − word bits (log2 K); use v = m for direct mapping
Speed-up from the cache = main-memory access time / average access time

notes.text: Bit-split recipe: word bits = log2(block size); direct: line bits = log2(lines); set-associative: set bits = log2(lines / k); fully associative: no index bits; tag = remaining bits. Doubling associativity removes one index bit and adds one tag bit.

Two formulas for average access time appear in books. Use t_avg = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m unless the question says memory is accessed only after the cache lookup fails, in which case the miss costs t_c + t_m.

Direct mapping needs no replacement algorithm and a single comparator; fully associative mapping needs a comparator per line (associative memory) and a replacement algorithm; set-associative needs k comparators and replacement within the set.

Write-back reduces bus traffic and uses a dirty bit; write-through keeps memory always up to date, which matters for DMA and multiprocessors. Write-allocate pairs naturally with write-back, no-write-allocate with write-through.

formulas.title: Average memory access time
formulas.plainText: t_avg = h × t_c + (1 − h) × t_m
formulas.description: With hit ratio h, cache time t_c and memory time t_m; for example h = 0.9, t_c = 10 ns, t_m = 100 ns gives 19 ns.

formulas.title: Number of lines and sets
formulas.plainText: m = C / K lines; v = m / k sets
formulas.description: A cache of C bytes with K-byte blocks has m lines; a k-way set-associative cache groups them into v sets, each indexed by log2 v address bits.

formulas.title: Tag field width
formulas.plainText: tag bits = A − log2(v) − log2(K)
formulas.description: Address bits left after the set (or line) index and the word offset; for a fully associative cache the index term is 0 and the tag is the whole block number.

formulas.title: Two-level cache access time
formulas.description: Average access time with an L1 and an L2 cache; the L2 term is weighted by the L1 miss ratio.

flashcards.front: A cache has 128 lines of 16 bytes and a 16-bit address. Give the tag/line/word split for direct mapping.
flashcards.back: Word = 4 bits (16 bytes), line = 7 bits (128 lines), tag = 16 − 7 − 4 = 5 bits.

flashcards.front: Compare write-through and write-back caches in one line each.
flashcards.back: Write-through writes every update to cache and main memory at once, keeping memory current at the cost of traffic; write-back writes only to the cache, marks the line dirty and updates memory when the line is evicted.

flashcards.front: Why do modern processors split the L1 cache but keep L2 unified?
flashcards.back: A split L1 lets the instruction-fetch and data stages of the pipeline access their own caches without contention; a unified L2 balances instruction and data space automatically for a higher hit ratio.

flashcards.front: Which mapping needs no replacement algorithm, and why?
flashcards.back: Direct mapping: each block has exactly one possible line (i = j mod m), so the resident block is always the one replaced; associative and set-associative caches must choose a victim (LRU, FIFO, LFU, random).

questions.questionText: A 4-way set-associative cache of 8 KB uses 32-byte blocks in a system with 32-bit byte addresses. The number of tag bits in the address is:
questions.explanation: Lines = 8192 / 32 = 256; sets = 256 / 4 = 64, so the set field is 6 bits and the word field is log2(32) = 5 bits. Tag = 32 − 6 − 5 = 21 bits.

questions.questionText: A program makes 2000 memory references, of which 1840 are found in the cache. What is the hit ratio?
questions.explanation: Hit ratio h = hits / total references = 1840 / 2000 = 0.92. The miss ratio is 1 − h = 160 / 2000 = 0.08.

questions.questionText: A cache has an access time of 5 ns, main memory has an access time of 80 ns, and the hit ratio is 0.95. Both are accessed simultaneously, so a hit takes 5 ns and a miss takes 80 ns in total. What is the average access time?
questions.explanation: Simultaneous model: t_avg = h t_c + (1 − h) t_m = 0.95 × 5 + 0.05 × 80 = 4.75 + 4 = 8.75 ns. Charging the cache time again on a miss (the hierarchical model) would give 5 + 0.05 × 80 = 9.00 ns.

questions.questionText: A processor looks in its cache (2 ns) first and accesses main memory (60 ns) only after a miss has been detected (hierarchical, look-through access). The hit ratio is 0.9. What is the average access time?
questions.explanation: Every access spends t_c and each miss adds t_m: t_avg = t_c + (1 − h) t_m = 2 + 0.1 × 60 = 8.0 ns, the same as 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × (2 + 60). The simultaneous model would give 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × 60 = 7.8 ns.

questions.questionText: A cache with an access time of 10 ns and a main memory with an access time of 50 ns are accessed simultaneously, so a miss costs 50 ns in total. What hit ratio is needed for an average access time of 18 ns?
questions.explanation: 18 = 10h + 50(1 − h) = 50 − 40h, so h = 32 / 40 = 0.80. With the hierarchical model, 18 = 10 + 50(1 − h), the answer would be 0.84 instead.

questions.questionText: A cache holds 32 KB of data in lines of 64 bytes (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many lines does it have?
questions.explanation: Lines m = cache size / line size = 32 × 1024 / 64 = 32,768 / 64 = 512. Taking 1 KB as 1000 bytes gives 500, and treating the 64-byte line as 64 bits gives 4096.

questions.questionText: In a byte-addressable memory, a cache uses 128-byte blocks. How many address bits form the word (byte-offset) field?
questions.explanation: The offset must select one of the 128 bytes of a block, so it needs log2(128) = 7 bits. Treating the 128 bytes as 1024 bits would wrongly give 10 bits.

questions.questionText: A 64 KB, 8-way set-associative cache uses 64-byte blocks (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many sets does it have?
questions.explanation: Lines = 65,536 / 64 = 1024, and sets = lines / ways = 1024 / 8 = 128, so the set field is 7 bits wide. 1024 is the number of lines, not the number of sets.

questions.questionText: How many tag comparisons are made in parallel on each access to a 4-way set-associative cache that has 256 sets?
questions.explanation: The set field selects one set, and only the 4 tags stored in that set are compared with the tag of the address, so 4 comparators are needed. A fully associative cache with the same 1024 lines would need 1024 comparisons, and a direct-mapped cache only 1.

questions.questionText: A cache has 8 lines and is organised as 8-way set-associative. This organisation is equivalent to:
options: A cache without a tag field
questions.explanation: With k = 8 ways and 8 lines there is v = 8 / 8 = 1 set, so any block can be placed in any line, which is fully associative mapping. At the other extreme, k = 1 (8 sets of one line) is direct mapping.

questions.questionText: Which cache mapping function needs no replacement algorithm?
questions.explanation: In direct mapping each block can go to exactly one line (block mod lines), so on a miss the block in that line is simply replaced and there is no choice to make. Associative and set-associative mappings must choose a victim using LRU, FIFO, LFU or random replacement.

questions.questionText: With fully associative mapping, the cache interprets a main-memory address as:
options: A tag field, a line field and a word field
A tag field, a set field and a word field
A line field and a word field only
A tag field and a word (offset) field only
questions.explanation: A block may be placed in any line, so there is nothing to index: the whole block number is the tag and is compared with the tags of all lines at once. Tag | line | word is direct mapping and tag | set | word is set-associative mapping.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped cache has 128 lines. Into which line is main-memory block number 300 placed?
questions.explanation: Direct mapping uses line = block mod lines = 300 mod 128 = 300 − 256 = 44. The quotient 300 div 128 = 2 is the tag stored with the line.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped cache stores 16 KB of data in 32-byte lines, and the processor uses 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). What are the widths of the tag, line and word fields?
questions.explanation: Word = log2(32) = 5 bits; lines = 16,384 / 32 = 512, so line = 9 bits; tag = 32 − 9 − 5 = 18 bits. Using log2 of the cache size in bytes (14) as the line field is a common slip.

questions.questionText: A fully associative cache of 64 KB with 16-byte lines is used with 24-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many bits wide is each tag?
questions.explanation: Fully associative mapping has no line or set field, so tag = address bits − word bits = 24 − log2(16) = 24 − 4 = 20 bits. A direct-mapped cache of the same size (4096 lines, 12 line bits) would need only 8 tag bits.

questions.questionText: A byte-addressable machine has 16-bit addresses, a 2 KB direct-mapped cache and 16-byte blocks, so an address is split as tag 5 | line 7 | word 4. Into which cache line is address 3A7C (hexadecimal) placed, and what tag is stored with it?
questions.explanation: 3A7C = 00111 0100111 1100 in binary, so the tag is 00111 = 7, the line is 0100111 = 39 and the word is 1100 = 12. Equivalently, block = 3A7 hex = 935, line = 935 mod 128 = 39 and tag = 935 div 128 = 7.

questions.questionText: A word-addressable main memory has 2^24 words of 32 bits. A direct-mapped cache holds 16K words (K = 1024) in blocks of 8 words. What are the widths of the tag, line and word fields of the address?
questions.explanation: The address selects a word, so it has 24 bits and the word field is log2(8) = 3 bits. Lines = 16K / 8 = 2048, giving 11 line bits, and tag = 24 − 11 − 3 = 10 bits; a 5-bit offset would apply only to byte addressing.

questions.questionText: A 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 32-byte blocks is used with 16-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Which address maps to the same cache line as address 1240 (hexadecimal) but belongs to a different memory block?
questions.explanation: There are 4096 / 32 = 128 lines, so an address splits as tag 4 | line 7 | word 5. 1240 hex is block 146, line 146 mod 128 = 18, tag 1; 3240 hex is block 402, line 402 mod 128 = 18, tag 3, so it competes for the same line. 1250 is inside the same block as 1240, and 1340 and 1640 map to lines 26 and 50.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped cache splits a 32-bit address as tag 16 | line 10 | word 6. The same cache, with the same total size and block size, is reorganised as 4-way set-associative. What are the new field widths?
questions.explanation: The 1024 lines in groups of 4 give 256 sets, so the set field is 8 bits; the block size is unchanged, so the word field stays 6 bits and tag = 32 − 8 − 6 = 18 bits. Each doubling of associativity moves one bit from the index to the tag.

questions.questionText: A 4-way set-associative cache holds 32 KB of data in 64-byte blocks, and the processor uses 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). For address 1234ABCD (hexadecimal), which set is selected and which tag is compared?
questions.explanation: Lines = 32,768 / 64 = 512 and sets = 512 / 4 = 128, so the fields are word 6, set 7 and tag 19 bits. Tag = address >> 13 = 91A5, set = (address >> 6) mod 128 = 2F and offset = 0D; using 8 set bits, as for 256 sets, would give set AF and tag 48D2.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped, write-through cache holds 32 KB of data in 64-byte lines for a processor with 32-bit byte addresses, and each line has one valid bit (1 KB = 1024 bytes). What is the total number of storage bits in the cache, including tags and valid bits?
questions.explanation: Lines = 32,768 / 64 = 512 (9 line bits), word = 6 bits and tag = 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits. Each line stores 64 × 8 = 512 data bits + 17 tag bits + 1 valid bit = 530 bits, so the total is 512 × 530 = 271,360 bits, about 3.5% more than the 262,144 data bits.

questions.questionText: A 2-way set-associative write-back cache holds 64 KB of data in 64-byte blocks for 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Each line stores a tag, a valid bit and a dirty bit (ignore replacement bits). How many bytes do the tags and status bits occupy in total?
questions.explanation: Lines = 65,536 / 64 = 1024 and sets = 512 (9 bits), word = 6 bits, so tag = 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits. Overhead = 1024 × (17 + 1 + 1) = 19,456 bits = 2432 bytes; a direct-mapped cache would need only 16 tag bits (2304 bytes), and leaving out the status bits gives 2176 bytes.

questions.questionText: The first reference ever made to a block always misses, whatever the size or organisation of the cache. Such a miss is called a:
questions.explanation: Compulsory misses occur because a block must be brought into the cache at its first use; only larger blocks or prefetching reduce them. Capacity misses come from a working set larger than the cache, and conflict misses from blocks competing for the same line or set.

questions.questionText: Which category of cache misses is eliminated completely by making a cache fully associative while keeping its size and block size unchanged?
questions.explanation: Conflict misses happen when blocks collide in one line or set while other lines are still usable; a fully associative cache can place a block anywhere, so they disappear. Compulsory and capacity misses depend on first use and on the cache size, not on placement.

questions.questionText: Which statement about cache size is NOT correct?
options: Doubling the cache size always halves the miss rate
A larger cache reduces capacity misses
Once the cache holds the program's working set, extra capacity gives diminishing returns
A larger cache tends to be slightly slower because of more address decoding and longer wires
questions.explanation: The miss rate falls as the cache grows, but with diminishing returns rather than in proportion; once the working set fits, doubling the size barely helps. The other three statements are standard design trade-offs.

questions.questionText: An array of 1024 four-byte integers, aligned to a block boundary, is read once in order a[0], a[1], …, a[1023]. The cache starts empty, is large enough to hold the whole array and uses 32-byte blocks. What is the miss rate of these reads?
questions.explanation: Each 32-byte block holds 8 integers, so only the first access to each block misses: 1024 / 8 = 128 misses out of 1024 reads = 12.5%. Dividing by the 4096 bytes instead of the 1024 reads gives 3.125%, and 16-byte blocks would give 25%.

questions.questionText: Two arrays A and B of 4-byte integers start at byte addresses 0 and 8192. A loop reads A[0], B[0], A[1], B[1], …, A[255], B[255]. The cache is 8 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) with 32-byte blocks and starts empty. What are the miss rates if the cache is direct-mapped, and if it is 2-way set-associative with LRU (same size and block size)?
questions.explanation: The 8192-byte offset is a multiple of the 8 KB cache size, so A[i] and B[i] fall in the same direct-mapped line and evict each other on every access: 100% misses. In the 2-way cache both blocks fit in one set, so only the first access to each 32-byte block (one in 8 elements) misses: 12.5%.

questions.questionText: Which replacement algorithm may evict a heavily used block simply because it was the first of the blocks in its set to be loaded?
questions.explanation: FIFO replaces the block that has been in the set longest, using only the order of loading and ignoring how often or how recently the block was used. LRU would keep a block that is being referenced repeatedly.

questions.questionText: Which statement about random replacement is correct?
options: It always gives a higher hit ratio than LRU
It can be used only with direct-mapped caches
It needs a counter in each line that is incremented on every reference
It picks the victim at random among the lines of the set, needs almost no bookkeeping hardware, and in simulations is only slightly worse than LRU
questions.explanation: Random replacement ignores the usage history, so it needs no age bits or counters, and simulation studies show its hit ratio is only slightly below that of usage-based algorithms. A per-line reference counter describes LFU.

questions.questionText: How can LRU replacement be implemented in a 2-way set-associative cache?
options: With a 2-bit counter per line that counts its accesses, replacing the line with the smaller count
With a single bit per set that records which of its two lines was referenced more recently; on a miss the other line is replaced
By always replacing the line that was loaded first, using a pointer in each set
It cannot be done in hardware, so the operating system must choose the victim
questions.explanation: With only two lines per set, one bit of state is enough to remember which line was used less recently (Stallings describes it as a USE bit in each line, set when the line is referenced while the other line's bit is cleared). The access counter describes LFU and the load-order pointer describes FIFO, neither of which is LRU.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines and starts empty. The processor references main-memory blocks in the order 0, 1, 4, 1, 0, 5, 1, 4, 2, 0. How many of these references are hits?
questions.explanation: Line = block mod 4, so blocks 0 and 4 share line 0 and blocks 1 and 5 share line 1: 0 M, 1 M, 4 M, 1 H, 0 M, 5 M, 1 M, 4 M, 2 M, 0 M. Only one reference hits; a 2-way LRU cache of the same size would score 4 hits.

questions.questionText: A 2-way set-associative cache with 4 sets and 16-byte blocks uses LRU replacement and starts empty. The processor reads byte addresses (hexadecimal) 000, 040, 004, 080, 010, 048, 000, 0C0, 014, 08C. How many hits occur, and which blocks does set 0 hold at the end?
questions.explanation: Block = address div 16 gives 0, 4, 0, 8, 1, 4, 0, 12, 1, 8, and set = block mod 4 puts all but block 1 in set 0. LRU: 0 M, 4 M, 0 H, 8 M (4 out), 1 M, 4 M (0 out), 0 M (8 out), 12 M (4 out), 1 H, 8 M (0 out), so 2 hits leave blocks 12 and 8 in set 0 (FIFO would score 3 hits).

questions.questionText: A fully associative cache with 3 lines starts empty. The processor references blocks 3, 4, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 1. How many hits occur with LRU and with FIFO replacement respectively?
questions.explanation: LRU: 3 M, 4 M, 2 M, 3 H, 4 H, 5 M (2 out), 3 H, 4 H, 5 H, 1 M, giving 5 hits. FIFO: 5 M evicts 3, the oldest block, then 3 M evicts 4 and 4 M evicts 2, followed by 5 H and 1 M, giving only 3 hits because FIFO discarded blocks still in use.

questions.questionText: In a write-back cache, when is a modified word copied to main memory?
options: When its cache line is replaced and the line's dirty bit is set
Immediately, on every write to the cache
Only when the program that wrote it terminates
On every clock cycle, by a background controller
questions.explanation: Write-back updates only the cache and sets the line's dirty (update) bit; main memory is written only when a dirty line is evicted. Writing memory on every write is write-through.

questions.questionText: Under a write-allocate policy, what happens on a write miss?
options: The word is written directly to main memory and the block is not loaded into the cache
The block containing the address is loaded into the cache and the write is then performed in the cache
The write is cancelled and retried after another block has been evicted
The whole cache is flushed to main memory before the write
questions.explanation: Write-allocate (fetch on write) brings the block in so that later accesses to it hit; it pairs naturally with write-back. Writing straight to memory without loading the block is no-write-allocate, also called write-around.

questions.questionText: A program writes the same cached variable 500 times and then its cache line is evicted. The line was already in the cache before the first write, and there is no write buffer or write combining. How many main-memory write operations occur with write-through and with write-back respectively?
questions.explanation: Write-through sends every write to memory: 500 writes. Write-back only sets the dirty bit on each write and copies the block to memory once, when the dirty line is evicted: 1 write.

questions.questionText: Which statement about cache write policies is correct?
options: Write-through needs a dirty bit in every line to know which lines must be copied back
With write-through, main memory always holds a current copy of every cached word, so a DMA device reading memory never sees stale data
Write-back causes more memory traffic than write-through when the same word is written many times
With write-back, an I/O module can safely read main memory directly without any cache-coherence measure
questions.explanation: Write-through updates memory on every write, keeping it valid for I/O modules and other bus masters at the cost of extra traffic. The dirty bit belongs to write-back, which writes each modified block once on eviction and can leave memory stale, so DMA needs snooping or a cache flush.

questions.questionText: A cache uses write-through with no-write-allocate and initially does not contain the block holding address X. The processor performs: write X, read X, read X, write X, read X. How many cache misses occur, and how many would occur with write-allocate instead?
questions.explanation: With no-write-allocate the first write misses and updates memory only, the next read misses and loads the block, and the remaining three accesses hit: 2 misses. With write-allocate the first write already loads the block, so only that access misses.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped, write-back, write-allocate cache has 4 lines and starts empty. The processor issues these accesses (operation and block number): R0, W0, R4, W4, R0, W5, R1, R8. How many cache misses occur, and how many dirty blocks are written back to main memory during the sequence?
questions.explanation: Line = block mod 4: R0 M; W0 H (dirty); R4 M, write back 0; W4 H (dirty); R0 M, write back 4; W5 M, allocated in line 1 and dirty; R1 M, write back 5; R8 M, but block 0 in line 0 is clean, so no write-back. That gives 6 misses and 3 write-backs.

questions.questionText: A write-back, write-allocate cache with 64-byte blocks serves 1,000,000 references with a miss rate of 2%. Every miss replaces a valid block, and 30% of the replaced blocks are dirty. How many bytes are transferred between the cache and main memory? (Ignore any other traffic.)
questions.explanation: Misses = 0.02 × 1,000,000 = 20,000, each fetching 64 bytes: 1,280,000 bytes. Dirty victims = 0.3 × 20,000 = 6000, each written back as 64 bytes: 384,000 bytes, so the total is 1,664,000 bytes (writing back every victim would give 2,560,000).

questions.questionText: The cache size is kept fixed while the block (line) size is increased step by step from very small to very large. Which statement is correct?
options: The hit ratio rises steadily, because every miss brings in more data
The hit ratio does not change; only the miss penalty changes
The hit ratio first rises because of spatial locality, then falls as fewer lines fit and useful blocks are evicted sooner, while the miss penalty keeps growing
The miss penalty falls, because fewer misses need to be serviced
questions.explanation: Larger blocks prefetch neighbouring words (spatial locality), but with a fixed size the number of lines drops, raising conflict and capacity misses, and each miss must transfer more bytes. The hit ratio therefore peaks at a moderate block size, 32 to 128 bytes in typical designs.

questions.questionText: On a cache miss, main memory needs 20 clock cycles before the first data appear; the 64-byte block is then transferred over an 8-byte-wide bus, one transfer per cycle. What is the miss penalty?
questions.explanation: Miss penalty = latency + (block size / bus width) × cycles per transfer = 20 + (64 / 8) × 1 = 20 + 8 = 28 cycles. Paying the 20-cycle latency again for each of the 8 transfers would give 8 × 21 = 168 cycles.

questions.questionText: Why do most processors use split level-1 caches (a separate instruction cache and data cache)?
options: Because a split cache always has a higher hit ratio than a unified cache of the same total size
Because instructions and data use different address widths
So that the pipeline can fetch an instruction and access data in the same cycle without competing for one cache
Because data must never be cached, only instructions
questions.explanation: A split (Harvard-style) L1 removes the structural hazard between the instruction-fetch stage and the memory-access stage. A unified cache of the same size balances its contents automatically and usually hits slightly more often, which is why L2 and L3 are unified.

questions.questionText: In a two-level cache, 5% of all processor references miss in L1, and 20% of the references that reach L2 miss there as well. What is the global miss rate of L2, the fraction of all processor references that must go to main memory?
questions.explanation: Global L2 miss rate = L1 miss rate × L2 local miss rate = 0.05 × 0.20 = 0.01 = 1%. The 20% is L2's local miss rate, and 4% (0.05 × 0.8) is the fraction of all references that hit in L2.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the design of a two-level cache hierarchy is correct?
options: L1 should be larger than L2 because it is closer to the processor
L1 is kept small and fast to minimise the hit time, while L2 is larger and often more associative to minimise the accesses that go to main memory
An L2 cache is useful only if it is faster than the L1 cache
Once an L2 cache is added, the L1 hit ratio no longer affects the average access time
questions.explanation: L1 sits on the processor's critical path, so its hit time limits the clock cycle; L2 exists to catch L1 misses before they pay the full memory penalty, so its size and associativity matter more than its speed.

questions.questionText: L1 hit time is 1 cycle and 4% of references miss in L1. L2 hit time is 10 cycles and its local miss rate is 25%. Main memory takes 100 cycles. Using AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty at each level, what is the average memory access time?
questions.explanation: L1 miss penalty = L2 hit time + L2 local miss rate × memory time = 10 + 0.25 × 100 = 35 cycles, so AMAT = 1 + 0.04 × 35 = 2.4 cycles. Without the L2 cache it would be 1 + 0.04 × 100 = 5.0 cycles.

questions.questionText: A processor has a base CPI of 1.2 with a perfect cache. Each instruction makes on average 1.5 memory references (one instruction fetch and 0.5 data references), 2% of all references miss in the cache, and the miss penalty is 50 cycles. What is the effective CPI?
questions.explanation: Memory-stall cycles per instruction = references per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty = 1.5 × 0.02 × 50 = 1.5, so CPI = 1.2 + 1.5 = 2.7, 2.25 times slower than with a perfect cache. Counting only the instruction fetches gives 1.2 + 1.0 = 2.2.

subtopics.title: Memory Write Ability, Permanence & Composing Memory
subtopics.subtitle: Write ability and permanence, composing wider and deeper memories, decoding, timing

concepts.text: Write Ability and Storage Permanence

Embedded-system designers (Vahid & Givargis) classify memories on two axes instead of the crude RAM-versus-ROM split. Write ability is the manner and speed in which a memory can be written: at one end sit memories that only the manufacturer can set, at the other memories the processor writes at full speed. Storage permanence is how long a memory holds its bits after they are written: from bits that last essentially forever to bits that leak away in milliseconds. Traditional ROM is the high-permanence, low-write-ability corner and traditional RAM is the opposite corner, but most real devices lie in between.
Write-ability spectrum, from lowest to highest:
items: Mask-programmed ROM: bits are fixed by a metal-layer mask during fabrication; not writable at all, cheapest per bit in volume.
OTP ROM / PROM: written once by blowing fuses with an external programmer.
EPROM: written by a programmer using high voltage, erased as a whole chip by ultraviolet light through a quartz window (minutes).
EEPROM: written electrically in-system, byte by byte, but each write takes microseconds to milliseconds and the chip must not be read during a write.
Flash: written electrically in-system in pages, erased in large blocks; faster bulk writes and higher density than EEPROM.
NVRAM: battery-backed SRAM, or SRAM paired with an EEPROM that saves its contents on power loss; written at processor speed.
SRAM and DRAM: written at processor speed with no practical limit on the number of writes.

concepts.text: Storage-permanence spectrum, from highest to lowest:
items: Mask ROM and OTP: hold data essentially forever with no power (nonvolatile, no erase cycles).
EPROM, EEPROM and flash: nonvolatile, but the stored charge leaks over years (about 10-year retention) and cells wear out after 10^3 to 10^6 program/erase cycles.
NVRAM: keeps data as long as its battery lasts or the backup EEPROM is intact.
SRAM: holds data only while powered (volatile) but needs no refresh.
DRAM: holds data for milliseconds only; needs refresh every few milliseconds even with power applied.
Nonvolatile memories are those on the high-permanence side of the line (they keep their bits without power); volatile ones lose them.

concepts.text: An in-system programmable memory can be written by the processor it is connected to without removing the chip from the board: EEPROM, flash, NVRAM and RAM qualify, while mask ROM, OTP and EPROM need an external programmer. In-system programmability makes field firmware updates, boot loaders, calibration tables and event logs possible. Flash has two practical constraints: a block must be erased (all bits set to 1) before any of its bytes can be rewritten, and writes are far slower than reads. Embedded systems therefore execute code directly from flash (execute-in-place) and keep changing data in SRAM, copying it to flash only occasionally.
Composing Memory

A system often needs a memory that is wider, deeper or both than any single available chip. Memory composition builds the required memory from several identical smaller chips. Three cases arise: increasing the width of each word, increasing the number of words, and increasing both. Every memory chip provides address inputs, bidirectional (tri-state) data lines and control inputs such as chip select (CS), output enable (OE) and read/write (R/W); composition is a matter of wiring these correctly.
Increasing the width (more bits per word):
items: Connect the chips in parallel: all chips receive the same address lines and the same CS, OE and R/W signals, so they are always accessed together.
Each chip supplies a slice of the data word: chip 0 drives data bits 0–7, chip 1 drives bits 8–15, and so on.
Number of chips = wanted width / chip width; the number of address lines does not change. Example: two 1K × 8 chips give a 1K × 16 memory.
Byte-enable signals can be added so that a single byte of the wide word can be written without disturbing the other chips.

concepts.text: Increasing the number of words (more depth):
items: Each chip holds a different range of addresses. The low-order address lines go to every chip in parallel; the high-order lines go to a decoder whose outputs drive the chip-select of exactly one chip.
The data lines of all chips are tied together; because outputs are tri-state, only the selected chip drives the bus.

Number of chips = wanted words / chip words; decoder size = log2(number of chips) inputs. Example: four 1K × 8 chips give 4K × 8 using address lines A0–A9 for every chip and a 2-to-4 decoder on A10–A11.
Total address lines = log2(total words); a 4K memory needs 12.

concepts.text: Increasing both width and depth:
items: Arrange the chips as a matrix: each row is one address range and the chips within a row are connected in parallel to supply the full word width.
The decoder on the high-order address bits selects one row; the low-order bits go to all chips; each column of chips drives its own slice of the data bus.
Chips needed = (words wanted / words per chip) × (width wanted / width per chip).

concepts.plainText: Chips = (total words × total bits per word) / (chip words × chip bits per word)

rows: Address lines of the composed memory
Selects one of the 4 rows via chip select
Each supplies 8 of the 16 data bits; both get the same CS

concepts.text: Memory Maps, Address Decoding and Timing

A memory map assigns a range of addresses to every memory chip and memory-mapped peripheral in the processor's address space; address decoding is the logic that activates the right chip select for each range. Full (absolute) decoding uses all address lines, so every location has exactly one address; partial decoding ignores some high-order lines, saving gates but making each device appear at several mirrored addresses (fold-back). A 3-to-8 decoder such as the 74LS138 is the classic building block: in a 64 KB space, an 8 KB ROM at 0000H–1FFFH is selected when A15 A14 A13 = 000, and an 8 KB RAM at 2000H–3FFFH when they are 001. The decoder can also carry the IO/M signal so that memory-mapped and isolated I/O ranges do not overlap.
Memory timing parameters:
items: Access time: for random-access memory, the time from presenting the address (or the read command) until valid data are available; for disk or tape, the time to position the head at the start.
Cycle time: the minimum time between two successive independent accesses; for DRAM it exceeds the access time because of precharge and the possibility of refresh; for SRAM the two are almost equal.
Transfer rate: for RAM, 1 / cycle time words per second; for a non-random device T_N = T_A + n / R, where n is the number of bits and R the rate in bits per second.

Wait states: if a memory's access time is longer than the processor allows in one bus cycle, the processor inserts idle clock cycles; wait states = ceil((t_access − t_allowed) / T_clk). Write cycles also need address setup and data hold times to be met.

concepts.plainText: Time to read n bits from a sequential device = average access time T_A + n / R

concepts.text: Embedded systems use the same hierarchy idea as general computers but with different priorities: cost, board space, power and predictable timing matter more than raw capacity. A typical microcontroller keeps its program in on-chip flash executed in place, its variables in on-chip SRAM, and its constants and calibration data in EEPROM or a flash data block; larger systems add external SDRAM for buffers and an SD card or serial flash for files. Caches appear only in higher-end embedded processors, because a cache miss makes execution time unpredictable; real-time designs therefore lock critical lines in the cache or use tightly coupled scratchpad memory that is addressed directly and always takes the same time. When external DRAM is used, a memory controller must generate the refresh cycles.
Going Deeper: Chip Pins, Composition and Decoding

A memory chip described as W × B holds W words of B bits, so it needs log2 W address pins, B data pins (usually bidirectional), a few control pins such as chip select (CS), output enable (OE) and write enable (WE), and power pins. The same number of bits can be organised in different ways: a 16-Kbit part may be 16K × 1 or 2K × 8, trading address pins for data pins. The 2K × 8 static RAM is a handy reference: 11 address pins, 8 data pins, 3 control pins and 2 power pins fit a 24-pin package. DRAMs halve the address pins by sending the row half and the column half of the address one after the other on the same pins.

concepts.plainText: Pins = log2(words) + data bits + control pins + power pins; for 2K × 8: 11 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 24

concepts.text: Why the composition rules work: one word of the composed memory is read in a single access, so all its bits must come from chips that are selected together, which is what a row of chips is. Different rows must hold different addresses, so a row is chosen by the address bits that the chips themselves do not use, decoded to one-of-R. Hence rows = total words ÷ words per chip, columns = word width ÷ chip width, the decoder has log2(rows) inputs, and the lowest log2(words per chip) address bits go to every chip.

Worked example 1: 16K x 16 memory from 4K x 4 chips (K = 1024)
rows    = 16K / 4K = 4          columns = 16 / 4 = 4
chips   = 4 x 4 = 16
address = log2(16384) = 14 lines, A13-A0 (word addresses)
to every chip : A11-A0 (log2 4096 = 12 lines)
decoder       : A13 A12 -> 2-to-4; output Yi = CS of all 4 chips in row i
data          : column j drives D(4j+3)-D(4j), j = 0..3
row 0: 0000H-0FFFH   row 1: 1000H-1FFFH
row 2: 2000H-2FFFH   row 3: 3000H-3FFFH

In a larger address space the high-order lines that the memory does not need must still be dealt with. Full decoding feeds every one of them into the chip-select logic, so each location has exactly one address. Partial decoding leaves m of them out; because the chip cannot tell their values apart, each location answers to 2^m addresses and the whole chip appears 2^m times (mirror images or fold-back). That is harmless as long as the images of different chips never overlap and software uses only one of them, but it blocks later expansion into the mirrored space. Linear select is the extreme case: one address line drives each chip select directly and no decoder is used at all.

concepts.plainText: Images = 2^(bus address lines − lines used inside the chip − lines used for chip select)

Worked example 2: 74LS138 in an 8085 system (A15-A0, 2 KB chips)
inputs  C B A = A13 A12 A11     enables G1 = 1, /G2A = A15, /G2B = A14
enabled only when A15 = A14 = 0  -> decoded window 0000H-3FFFH
Y0: 0000H-07FFH   Y1: 0800H-0FFFH   Y2: 1000H-17FFH   Y3: 1800H-1FFFH
Y4: 2000H-27FFH   Y5: 2800H-2FFFH   Y6: 3000H-37FFH   Y7: 3800H-3FFFH
